name: SQL
desc: The gap that costs most people offers. Every topic covered at interview depth — syntax, gotchas, edge cases, and the "why" behind each concept.
tip: If you blank on syntax, narrate your logic out loud — 'I'd partition by department, rank by salary descending, filter where rank = 1.' Interviewers weight reasoning as much as the final query.

r: RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3). DENSE_RANK does not (1,1,2).
WHERE runs before GROUP BY — cannot use aggregates. HAVING runs after.
Re-evaluates for every outer row. Slow on large data.
LEFT JOIN + WHERE on right column
Drops NULLs → becomes INNER JOIN. Move filter to ON clause.
NOT IN returns zero rows if subquery has any NULL. Use NOT EXISTS.
CROSS APPLY can reference outer columns in inner query. JOIN cannot.
Row versioning — readers never block writers. Enable at DB level.
Include all queried columns in the index to avoid Key Lookups.

days.title: Joins — all types, algorithms, and the hidden traps
days.exp: Joins are the most-tested SQL topic. At interview depth, it's not enough to know the types — you must understand the hidden LEFT JOIN + WHERE trap, when to use CROSS/OUTER APPLY, and how the optimizer chooses join algorithms. Each of these appears in senior-level rounds.
pts: INNER JOIN — only matching rows from both sides; non-matching rows from either side are dropped entirely
LEFT JOIN — all rows from left table; right side is NULL where no match exists
RIGHT JOIN — all rows from right table; left side is NULL where no match exists
FULL OUTER JOIN — all rows from both sides; NULLs on whichever side had no match
CROSS JOIN — Cartesian product: every row in A paired with every row in B; use with care (N×M rows)
SELF JOIN — table joined to itself with two aliases; classic for employee-manager hierarchies
**LEFT JOIN + WHERE trap:** `WHERE t2.col = x` on a LEFT JOIN drops all NULL rows silently, turning it into an INNER JOIN. Move the filter to the `ON` clause to preserve outer-join behaviour

**CROSS APPLY:** like CROSS JOIN but the inner query can reference columns from the outer query; equivalent to INNER JOIN for set-returning functions; useful for top-N per group without a window function
**OUTER APPLY:** like CROSS APPLY but preserves outer rows with no inner match (equivalent to LEFT JOIN for set-returning functions)
**Join algorithms:** optimizer chooses Nested Loop (small sets / indexed lookups), Hash Join (large unordered sets), or Merge Join (both inputs sorted on join key). Visible in the execution plan.
Implicit JOIN syntax (`FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.id`) is old-style — always use explicit JOIN keywords for clarity
**Multi-table joins:** the optimizer can reorder joins freely; the written order affects readability, not semantics (unless hints are used)
days.code:
-- LEFT JOIN trap: accidentally becomes INNER JOIN
SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'IN';              -- ❌ drops NULL rows (no customer match)

-- Fix: move filter into ON
SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id AND c.country = 'IN'; -- ✓

-- SELF JOIN: employee with manager name
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

-- CROSS APPLY: top 1 most recent order per customer
SELECT c.name, o.order_date, o.total
FROM customers c
CROSS APPLY (
  SELECT TOP 1 order_date, total
  FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY order_date DESC
) o;   -- CROSS APPLY can reference c.id — a JOIN cannot do this

-- OUTER APPLY: same but keep customers with no orders
SELECT c.name, o.order_date, o.total
FROM customers c
OUTER APPLY (
  SELECT TOP 1 order_date, total
  FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY order_date DESC
) o;   -- NULL for order_date/total where no orders exist

qa.q: What is the LEFT JOIN + WHERE trap and how do you fix it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** When you filter on a right-table column in the WHERE clause of a LEFT JOIN, you drop all the NULL-producing rows because NULL ≠ any value. This silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. Fix: move the filter from WHERE to the ON clause so rows with no match are preserved with NULL values in the right-side columns.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What is the difference between CROSS APPLY and CROSS JOIN?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** CROSS JOIN pairs every row from two static tables — neither side can reference the other. CROSS APPLY executes a table expression (a subquery or function) for each row of the left input, and that expression CAN reference columns from the outer (left) row. APPLY is essential for top-N per group and calling table-valued functions per row.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What are the three join algorithms SQL Server uses and when does the optimizer choose each?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Nested Loop: for small inputs or when the inner side has an index on the join key — O(n×log m). Hash Join: for large inputs with no useful index — builds a hash table from the smaller input, probes with the larger. Merge Join: when both inputs are already sorted on the join key — most efficient if data is pre-sorted. The optimizer chooses based on estimated row counts and available indexes.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: When would you use a SELF JOIN and what is the alternative?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SELF JOIN when you need to compare or link rows within the same table — classic: employee-manager hierarchy. The alternative for modern hierarchies is a recursive CTE, which handles arbitrary depth without multiple self-joins. SELF JOIN is simpler for a single level (employee and their direct manager); recursive CTE is needed for a full tree traversal.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What is OUTER APPLY and when do you use it instead of LEFT JOIN?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** OUTER APPLY executes an inner table expression per outer row and preserves outer rows with no inner match (like LEFT JOIN). Use OUTER APPLY when the inner expression references the outer row's columns (which a LEFT JOIN cannot do), or when calling a table-valued function per row — for example, getting the most recent order per customer while keeping customers with no orders.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

days.title: Aggregation — GROUP BY, HAVING, ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS
days.exp: The basics (GROUP BY/HAVING) are tested in every SQL round. At 4 YOE you're also expected to know ROLLUP and CUBE for reporting queries, STRING_AGG for string aggregation, and the exact logical execution order that explains every 'why can I use this here?' question.
pts: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows including NULLs; `COUNT(col)` counts only non-NULL values in that column
SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX all silently ignore NULL values — important for correctness
`GROUP BY` collapses rows into groups; every SELECT column must be either in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function
`HAVING` filters groups after aggregation — can use aggregates; `WHERE` filters rows before — cannot
Logical execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY (memorise this)
**ROLLUP:** `GROUP BY ROLLUP(a, b)` generates subtotals for (a,b), (a), and () — hierarchical subtotals plus grand total
**CUBE:** `GROUP BY CUBE(a, b)` generates all combinations: (a,b), (a), (b), () — all possible subtotals
**GROUPING SETS:** `GROUP BY GROUPING SETS((a,b),(a),())` — explicitly define which groupings you want (most flexible)
**GROUPING(col):** returns 1 when the column is being aggregated into a subtotal (NULL in ROLLUP/CUBE output), 0 otherwise — lets you distinguish real NULLs from rollup NULLs
**STRING_AGG(col, separator):** aggregate string values into a delimited list (SQL Server 2017+)
**COUNT(*) OVER():** window aggregate — count without collapsing rows; combines aggregation with window functions
days.code:
-- Basics
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS hc, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal, MAX(salary) AS top_sal
FROM employees
WHERE active = 1
GROUP BY dept
HAVING AVG(salary) > 70000
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC;

-- ROLLUP: subtotals per dept, then grand total
SELECT dept, job_title, SUM(salary) AS total_sal
FROM employees
GROUP BY ROLLUP(dept, job_title);
-- rows: (Eng, SWE), (Eng, Mgr), (Eng, NULL=subtotal), (Sales, ...), (NULL, NULL=grand total)

-- GROUPING() to label subtotal rows
SELECT
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(dept) = 1 THEN 'ALL DEPTS' ELSE dept END AS dept,
  CASE WHEN GROUPING(job_title) = 1 THEN 'ALL ROLES' ELSE job_title END AS role,
  SUM(salary) AS total
FROM employees
GROUP BY ROLLUP(dept, job_title);

-- GROUPING SETS: only the groupings you need
SELECT dept, job_title, SUM(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS((dept, job_title), (dept), ());

-- STRING_AGG: comma-separated employee list per dept
SELECT dept, STRING_AGG(name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY name) AS members
FROM employees GROUP BY dept;

qa.q: What is the logical SQL execution order and why does it matter?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. This explains: (1) you cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE because SELECT hasn't run yet, (2) you cannot use aggregates in WHERE because GROUP BY hasn't run yet, (3) you CAN use SELECT aliases in ORDER BY. Knowing this order lets you reason about any SQL clause rule.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is the difference between ROLLUP, CUBE, and GROUPING SETS?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ROLLUP generates hierarchical subtotals plus a grand total — GROUP BY ROLLUP(a,b) gives (a,b), (a), and (). CUBE generates ALL combinations of subtotals — GROUP BY CUBE(a,b) gives (a,b), (a), (b), and (). GROUPING SETS lets you specify exactly which groupings you want, making it the most flexible and explicit. Use ROLLUP for hierarchical reports, CUBE for pivot-table-like analysis, GROUPING SETS when you need a specific subset of groupings.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: How do you distinguish a rollup NULL from a real NULL in a ROLLUP/CUBE query?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use the GROUPING(col) function — it returns 1 when the column is being used in a subtotal aggregation (meaning the NULL was generated by ROLLUP/CUBE), and 0 when the column has a real value or a real NULL. Use CASE WHEN GROUPING(dept) = 1 THEN 'Grand Total' ELSE dept END to label subtotal rows.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What does STRING_AGG do and what is its syntax?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** STRING_AGG(column, separator) concatenates all non-NULL values of column within each group into a single delimited string — like Python's ','.join(). Available in SQL Server 2017+. Add WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY col) to control the order of concatenated values. Example: STRING_AGG(name, ', ') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY name) produces an alphabetical comma-separated list.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: Why does COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(column)?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** COUNT(*) counts every row including those with NULLs in any column. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that specific column is NOT NULL. If salary has 10 rows but 2 are NULL: COUNT(*) = 10, COUNT(salary) = 8. This matters for accurate reporting — use COUNT(*) for total rows, COUNT(col) when NULLs should be excluded from the count.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

days.title: Subqueries — scalar, correlated, APPLY operators, EXISTS vs IN
days.exp: Subqueries test your understanding of SQL execution and NULL semantics. The NOT IN NULL trap is a real production bug waiting to happen. CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY unlock the 'top N per group' pattern that trips up many candidates.
pts: Scalar subquery: returns exactly one value, usable anywhere a single value is expected (SELECT, WHERE, HAVING)
Non-correlated subquery: independent of outer query, executes once, result reused
Correlated subquery: references outer query columns, **re-executes for every outer row** — potentially O(n × m)
`EXISTS` short-circuits at first match; `IN` materialises the full result set first — EXISTS is usually faster for large sets
**NOT IN NULL trap:** if the subquery returns ANY NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row → zero rows returned. Three-valued logic in action.
**NOT EXISTS** does not have the NULL trap — it checks for absence of matching rows and handles NULLs correctly
**CROSS APPLY:** correlated join to a table expression; preserves all outer rows that produce at least one inner row (like INNER JOIN)
**OUTER APPLY:** correlated join that preserves all outer rows even if inner expression returns nothing (like LEFT JOIN)
Top-N per group with APPLY: apply a `SELECT TOP N ... WHERE id = outer.id ORDER BY ...` per outer row — cleaner than a CTE with window functions for some patterns
Rewrite correlated subqueries to JOINs or window functions for better performance at scale
days.code:
-- NOT IN NULL trap: returns zero rows if any customer_id is NULL!
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);  -- ❌ dangerous

-- Safe alternative 1: NOT EXISTS
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id); -- ✓

-- Safe alternative 2: LEFT JOIN + IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;  -- ✓ also works

-- Correlated subquery: employees earning > dept average
SELECT name, salary, dept FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
  WHERE dept = e.dept  -- correlated: re-runs for each outer row
);
-- Faster rewrite using window function:
SELECT name, salary, dept FROM (
  SELECT *, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
) t WHERE salary > dept_avg;

-- CROSS APPLY: most recent order per customer
SELECT c.id, c.name, latest.order_date, latest.total
FROM customers c
CROSS APPLY (
  SELECT TOP 1 order_date, total
  FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY order_date DESC
) latest;

-- EXISTS vs IN: EXISTS is faster when subquery is large
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 1000);

qa.q: What is the NOT IN NULL trap and how do you fix it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If a subquery used with NOT IN returns any NULL, then every row in the outer query evaluates to UNKNOWN (due to three-valued logic) and is filtered out — returning zero rows total. Fix: use NOT EXISTS instead, which checks for the absence of matching rows and handles NULLs correctly. Alternatively, add WHERE col IS NOT NULL to the subquery, but NOT EXISTS is safer and clearer.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: When should you use EXISTS over IN and why?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** EXISTS short-circuits — it stops as soon as it finds the first matching row. IN materialises the entire result set. For large subquery results, EXISTS is typically faster. EXISTS also handles NULLs correctly (no NULL trap). Use IN when: the subquery result is small, you want a list of static values (IN (1,2,3)), or the NOT IN case when you've confirmed no NULLs exist.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: How would you rewrite a correlated subquery for better performance?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Most correlated subqueries can be rewritten as: (1) a JOIN with aggregation in a derived table or CTE, or (2) a window function. Example: instead of WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = e.dept), use AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) in a subquery/CTE then filter in the outer query. Window functions are usually faster because they make a single pass over the data.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What is the difference between CROSS APPLY and CROSS JOIN?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** CROSS JOIN combines two independent tables — neither side can reference the other. CROSS APPLY executes an inner table expression FOR EACH row of the outer table, and that expression CAN reference outer columns. This makes CROSS APPLY essential for calling table-valued functions per row, or for top-N per group queries where the inner SELECT uses a TOP N ... WHERE id = outer.id pattern.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What are the three ways to write "find customers who have never placed an order"?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1) NOT EXISTS (safest): WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id). 2) LEFT JOIN + IS NULL: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL. 3) NOT IN (risky): WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) — fails silently if customer_id can be NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

days.title: NULL handling, string functions, date functions — complete reference
days.exp: NULLs propagate through expressions and break comparisons silently. String and date functions are tested constantly because they appear in real-world reporting queries. Know when each function is appropriate — interviewers often give a scenario and ask which function you would reach for.
pts: `ISNULL(col, default)` — SQL Server only, exactly 2 args, replaces NULL with default
`COALESCE(a, b, c...)` — ANSI standard, returns first non-NULL from any number of args; type resolution uses highest-precedence type
`NULLIF(a, b)` — returns NULL if a = b, else returns a; classic use: safe division `total / NULLIF(count, 0)`
`IIF(condition, true_val, false_val)` — shorthand CASE WHEN for simple conditions
`TRY_CONVERT(type, value)` / `TRY_CAST(value AS type)` — return NULL on conversion failure instead of raising an error

**String functions:** `LEN` (length), `TRIM`/`LTRIM`/`RTRIM`, `UPPER`/`LOWER`, `SUBSTRING(str, start, len)`, `CHARINDEX(find, str)`, `REPLACE(str, old, new)`, `STUFF(str, start, len, replacement)`, `FORMAT(val, format)`

**Date functions:** `GETDATE()` (now), `GETUTCDATE()` (UTC now), `DATEDIFF(unit, start, end)`, `DATEADD(unit, n, date)`, `DATEPART(unit, date)`, `EOMONTH(date)` (last day of month), `DATEFROMPARTS(y,m,d)`
`FORMAT(val, 'pattern')` — flexible formatting for display (slow; avoid in WHERE clauses)
`CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` — conditional column logic; can be nested and used in ORDER BY, GROUP BY, WHERE
**NULL comparison rules:** NULL = NULL → NULL (unknown), not TRUE. Always use `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`
days.code:
-- COALESCE vs ISNULL
SELECT COALESCE(mobile, home_phone, 'no contact') AS phone FROM employees;
SELECT ISNULL(salary, 0) AS salary FROM employees;  -- SQL Server only, 2 args

-- NULLIF: safe division to avoid divide-by-zero
SELECT orders, revenue / NULLIF(orders, 0) AS avg_order_value FROM daily_stats;

-- TRY_CONVERT: handle invalid data gracefully
SELECT TRY_CONVERT(INT, user_input) AS safe_int FROM raw_data;
-- Returns NULL instead of error for 'abc' input

-- String functions
SELECT
  LEN(name) AS name_len,
  UPPER(LEFT(name, 1)) + LOWER(SUBSTRING(name, 2, 100)) AS title_case,
  CHARINDEX('@', email) AS at_pos,
  REPLACE(description, 'old_term', 'new_term') AS updated,
  TRIM(BOTH ' ' FROM ' hello ') AS trimmed   -- SQL Server 2017+
FROM employees;

-- Date functions
SELECT
  GETDATE() AS now,
  DATEDIFF(YEAR, hire_date, GETDATE()) AS years_at_company,
  DATEADD(MONTH, 3, GETDATE()) AS next_quarter,
  EOMONTH(GETDATE()) AS end_of_month,
  DATEPART(WEEKDAY, order_date) AS day_of_week,
  DATEFROMPARTS(2024, 12, 31) AS specific_date
FROM employees;

-- CASE WHEN in ORDER BY
SELECT name, status FROM tasks
ORDER BY CASE status WHEN 'urgent' THEN 1 WHEN 'high' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END;

qa.q: What is the difference between ISNULL and COALESCE?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ISNULL is SQL Server-specific and takes exactly 2 arguments. COALESCE is ANSI SQL standard, accepts multiple arguments (returning the first non-NULL), and uses different type-resolution rules (highest-precedence type wins across all arguments). For portability and multi-argument fallback chains, prefer COALESCE. ISNULL is slightly faster in micro-benchmarks but the difference is rarely significant.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is NULLIF and what problem does it solve?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a equals b, otherwise returns a. Its primary use is safe division: revenue / NULLIF(orders, 0) — when orders is 0, NULLIF returns NULL, and dividing by NULL gives NULL (not an error). Without NULLIF, a zero denominator raises a divide-by-zero error. It also appears in data cleaning to replace sentinel values (like -1 meaning "not applicable") with NULL.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is TRY_CONVERT and when should you use it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** TRY_CONVERT(type, value) attempts a data type conversion and returns NULL on failure instead of raising an error. Use it when processing user input, importing data from external sources, or querying columns that should be typed but aren't. Example: TRY_CONVERT(INT, user_input) returns NULL for 'abc' instead of crashing. Regular CONVERT or CAST will raise an error in the same scenario.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What are the most important string functions to know for T-SQL interviews?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SUBSTRING(str, start, len) — extract a portion. CHARINDEX(find, str) — position of a substring (0 if not found). LEN(str) — length (excludes trailing spaces). REPLACE(str, old, new) — global replacement. STUFF(str, start, len, replacement) — delete then insert. LTRIM/RTRIM/TRIM — remove whitespace. UPPER/LOWER — case conversion. LEFT(str, n) / RIGHT(str, n) — take n characters from each end.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: How do you handle NULL values in WHERE comparisons?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** NULL is never equal to anything, including itself — NULL = NULL evaluates to NULL (unknown), not TRUE. WHERE col = NULL never returns any rows; WHERE col != NULL also returns nothing. Always use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. For functions: COALESCE(col, fallback) = x will work for comparisons because COALESCE replaces NULL before the comparison. Failing to handle NULLs in WHERE is a common source of "missing rows" bugs.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

days.title: Set operations, query rewriting, and performance patterns
days.exp: Set operations are tested as much for understanding SQL as a set-based language as for the syntax itself. The NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS distinction saves bugs. Query rewriting — turning a subquery into a JOIN or window function — is a genuine 4-YOE interview topic.
pts: `UNION` deduplicates (sort/hash step); `UNION ALL` keeps all rows — always faster, use when duplicates are safe or impossible
`INTERSECT` — rows appearing in BOTH result sets (like an implicit INNER JOIN on all columns)
`EXCEPT` — rows in the first set NOT in the second (safer than NOT IN for NULL handling)
All set operators require: same number of columns, compatible data types; column names come from the first query
**Rewrite subquery → JOIN:** `WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)` → `JOIN orders ON id = customer_id`; usually faster with large sets
**Rewrite correlated subquery → window function:** correlated `SELECT AVG(salary) WHERE dept = e.dept` → `AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept)`; single scan
**Rewrite DISTINCT → GROUP BY:** sometimes GROUP BY has better execution plan for certain indexes
EXCEPT handles NULLs correctly (two NULLs are considered equal); NOT IN does not
UNION vs OR in WHERE: `WHERE a=1 UNION SELECT * WHERE b=2` is sometimes faster than `WHERE a=1 OR b=2` because the optimizer can use separate index seeks
days.code:
-- UNION (dedup) vs UNION ALL (fast, keeps dups)
SELECT email FROM active_users
UNION ALL    -- use ALL unless you specifically need deduplication
SELECT email FROM archived_users;

-- INTERSECT: users active in BOTH Jan and Feb
SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE MONTH(date)=1
INTERSECT
SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE MONTH(date)=2;

-- EXCEPT: users who ordered Jan but NOT Feb (NULL-safe)
SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE MONTH(date)=1
EXCEPT
SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE MONTH(date)=2;

-- Rewrite IN subquery → JOIN (often faster)
-- Slow:
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1000);
-- Faster:
SELECT DISTINCT c.name FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.total > 1000;

-- Rewrite correlated subquery → window function
-- Slow (O(n²)):
SELECT name, salary FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = e.dept);
-- Fast (single scan):
SELECT name, salary FROM (
  SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
) t WHERE salary > dept_avg;

qa.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** UNION removes duplicate rows by performing a sort or hash operation across the combined result set — extra CPU and memory cost. UNION ALL keeps all rows including duplicates and skips the deduplication step — significantly faster. Always use UNION ALL unless you specifically need deduplication. If the two queries select from different tables or have different WHERE conditions that guarantee no duplicates, UNION ALL is the correct choice.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: How does EXCEPT handle NULLs differently from NOT IN?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** EXCEPT uses set semantics where two NULLs are considered EQUAL — a NULL in set A matches a NULL in set B, so that row is excluded from the result. NOT IN uses three-valued logic where NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, meaning any NULL in the subquery causes ALL outer rows to be filtered out. For "rows in A not in B" comparisons, EXCEPT or NOT EXISTS are both NULL-safe; NOT IN is not.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: When would you rewrite a subquery to a JOIN?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** When the subquery is in an IN clause or a correlated subquery used for filtering, a JOIN often produces a better execution plan because: (1) the optimizer can push predicates more freely, (2) it can use hash or merge join algorithms efficiently, and (3) it avoids re-executing the subquery per row. However, be careful: subquery → JOIN can return duplicate outer rows if the inner table has multiple matches. Use DISTINCT or EXISTS to preserve the original cardinality.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: How would you rewrite a correlated subquery to a window function?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Move the correlated computation into a window function in a derived table or CTE, then filter in the outer query. Example: WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = e.dept) becomes WITH cte AS (SELECT *, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg FROM employees) SELECT * FROM cte WHERE salary > dept_avg. This makes one pass over the table instead of re-scanning per row.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: What is a practical use case for UNION (not UNION ALL)?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** When you genuinely need to deduplicate across two sources — for example, merging email lists from two systems and needing one unique entry per address, or finding the distinct set of users who appeared in either a paid or a free tier at any point. If you need the count of total records (including duplicates), use UNION ALL. If you need distinct records across both sets, use UNION.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

days.title: Nth highest salary — 3 approaches + classic problems
days.exp: The Nth highest salary problem is asked so often because it has three distinct solutions representing three SQL paradigms. After solving it three ways, practice the 'second highest salary with NULL return' variant — that edge case reveals whether you truly understand each approach.
pts: Approach 1: `OFFSET FETCH` — clean, readable, SQL Server 2012+; but returns empty set (not NULL) when N does not exist
Approach 2: Correlated subquery with `COUNT(DISTINCT salary)` — works everywhere; slowest O(n²)
Approach 3: `DENSE_RANK()` — most robust; handles ties and non-existence correctly
**RANK vs DENSE_RANK for Nth highest:** RANK leaves gaps after ties (1,1,3) — rank 2 may not exist. DENSE_RANK has no gaps (1,1,2) — every rank N is always reachable
**Edge case: return NULL not empty set** — wrap in SELECT with ISNULL or use outer query: `SELECT MAX(salary) WHERE rnk = N` returns NULL when N does not exist
**Nth highest per group:** `DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)` then filter WHERE rnk = N
Practice: "second highest salary or NULL if it does not exist" — a very common variant that tests edge case handling
days.code:
-- Problem: find the 3rd highest distinct salary

-- Approach 1: OFFSET FETCH (clean but empty set if N doesn't exist)
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC
OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROW ONLY;

-- Approach 2: Correlated subquery
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees e
WHERE (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM employees
  WHERE salary > e.salary
) = 2;   -- exactly 2 distinct salaries are higher → this is 3rd

-- Approach 3: DENSE_RANK (most robust — handles ties + non-existence)
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t WHERE rnk = 3;

-- Variant: return NULL if 3rd highest doesn't exist
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t WHERE rnk = 3;   -- MAX of empty set = NULL ✓

-- Nth highest PER DEPARTMENT
SELECT dept, salary FROM (
  SELECT dept, salary,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
) t WHERE rnk = 2;

qa.q: What are the three approaches to Nth highest salary and when would you choose each?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** OFFSET FETCH: cleanest syntax, best for simple cases, but returns empty set (not NULL) when N doesn't exist. Correlated subquery: works everywhere, most portable, but O(n²) — avoid on large tables. DENSE_RANK: most robust, handles ties correctly, O(n log n), can be adapted to return NULL for non-existent ranks. In interviews, lead with DENSE_RANK and explain why — it shows the deepest understanding.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: Why does DENSE_RANK handle the Nth highest problem better than RANK?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** RANK leaves gaps after ties — if two employees share salary rank 1, the next rank is 3 (not 2). So rank 2 doesn't exist and a query for the "2nd highest" returns nothing. DENSE_RANK has no gaps — next after tied rank 1 is rank 2, every rank N is always reachable. For finding the Nth distinct salary, DENSE_RANK is the semantically correct choice.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: How do you make the Nth highest query return NULL instead of an empty set when N doesn't exist?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Wrap the DENSE_RANK query in MAX(salary): SELECT MAX(salary) FROM (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM employees) t WHERE rnk = N. When no rows match, MAX of an empty set returns NULL. This is the standard approach for the "second highest salary or NULL" variant on LeetCode.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: How do you find the Nth highest salary per department in a single query?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SELECT dept, salary FROM (SELECT dept, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM employees) t WHERE rnk = N; The PARTITION BY dept resets the rank counter per department, so rank 1 is the highest salary within each department separately.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: What is the time complexity of the correlated subquery approach vs DENSE_RANK?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Correlated subquery is O(n²): for each of the n outer rows, the subquery scans all n rows to count higher salaries. DENSE_RANK (window function) requires a sort — O(n log n). For large tables, the correlated subquery approach can be dramatically slower. OFFSET FETCH with DISTINCT also requires a sort — O(n log n). DENSE_RANK is generally the most efficient approach.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

days.title: Window functions part 1 — ranking, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK
days.exp: Window functions are the #1 gap that fails .NET/backend devs in SQL rounds. Master the ranking functions, know the differences cold, and understand NTILE for percentile bucketing — all of these appear in analytics and reporting interviews.
pts: **OVER() clause:** defines the window. PARTITION BY resets per group (like GROUP BY but keeps rows). ORDER BY inside OVER() defines sort order within the window.
`ROW_NUMBER()` — always unique (1,2,3,4), even for ties — arbitrary tiebreaking unless ORDER BY is deterministic
`RANK()` — tied values share a rank; **gaps appear after ties** (1,1,3,4) — gap = number of tied rows
`DENSE_RANK()` — tied values share a rank; **no gaps** (1,1,2,3) — preferred for Nth value problems
`NTILE(n)` — divides the result set into n equally-sized buckets; returns the bucket number for each row. Uneven splits give extra row to earlier buckets.
`PERCENT_RANK()` — rank as a percentage: (rank - 1) / (total rows - 1). Returns 0 for lowest, 1 for highest.
`CUME_DIST()` — cumulative distribution: proportion of rows with values ≤ current value
Window functions execute AFTER WHERE and GROUP BY — to filter on a window function result, wrap in CTE or subquery
You can use multiple window functions with different OVER() specifications in the same SELECT
days.code:
SELECT name, dept, salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)   AS rn,
  RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)   AS rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC)   AS drnk,
  NTILE(4)     OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary ASC)    AS quartile,
  PERCENT_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary)      AS pct_rank,
  CUME_DIST()    OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary)      AS cum_dist
FROM employees;

-- Top earner per department using ROW_NUMBER
SELECT name, dept, salary FROM (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn
  FROM employees
) t WHERE rn = 1;  -- id as tiebreaker makes row_number deterministic

-- Top 3 per dept INCLUDING ties (use DENSE_RANK)
SELECT name, dept, salary FROM (
  SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM employees
) t WHERE drnk <= 3;

-- NTILE: assign salary quartile labels
SELECT name, salary,
  CASE NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary)
    WHEN 1 THEN 'Q1 (bottom 25%)'
    WHEN 2 THEN 'Q2'
    WHEN 3 THEN 'Q3'
    WHEN 4 THEN 'Q4 (top 25%)'
  END AS quartile
FROM employees;

-- Can't use window function in WHERE — must wrap
-- WRONG: WHERE DENSE_RANK() OVER (...) <= 3
-- RIGHT:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rnk <= 3;

qa.q: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ROW_NUMBER: always assigns unique sequential numbers — even tied rows get different numbers (tiebreaking is arbitrary unless the ORDER BY is deterministic). RANK: tied rows share the same rank, but the next rank after a tie jumps (1,1,3 — a gap equal to the number of tied rows). DENSE_RANK: tied rows share the same rank, the next rank after a tie is consecutive with no gap (1,1,2). Use DENSE_RANK for "Nth highest" problems; ROW_NUMBER for "exactly one row per group."

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: What does NTILE(4) do and how does it handle uneven splits?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** NTILE(4) divides the result set into 4 equally-sized buckets and assigns each row a bucket number 1–4. For 10 rows split into 4 buckets: buckets 1 and 2 get 3 rows each, buckets 3 and 4 get 2 rows each (extra rows go to earlier buckets). NTILE is useful for assigning percentile labels (quartiles, deciles) without a separate PERCENTILE calculation.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: What is PERCENT_RANK and what values does it return?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** PERCENT_RANK() = (rank - 1) / (total rows - 1). It returns 0 for the row with the lowest ORDER BY value and 1 for the highest. For a dataset with 5 rows: the ranks 1,2,3,4,5 become 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. It answers "what percentage of rows have a value less than or equal to this row." Useful for normalizing rankings to a 0-1 scale.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: How do you use two different window functions with different partitions in the same query?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Each OVER() clause is independent — you can define different PARTITION BY and ORDER BY for each window function in the same SELECT. Example: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) ranks within dept, while RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) ranks globally across all employees — both computed in the same query without any subquery.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: Why can you not use a window function directly in a WHERE clause?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Window functions are evaluated in the SELECT phase, which comes AFTER WHERE in the logical execution order (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY). By the time SELECT runs (and window functions are computed), WHERE has already filtered the rows. To filter on a window function result, wrap the query in a CTE or subquery so the outer WHERE can reference the computed column.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

days.title: Window functions part 2 — LAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, running totals, frames
days.exp: LAG/LEAD replace self-joins for consecutive-row comparisons. FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE with the right frame are frequently misused — the default frame often gives unexpected results. Running totals and moving averages test whether you understand the ROWS BETWEEN frame clause.
pts: `LAG(col, n, default)` — value n rows before current in the window partition; default returned when no prior row exists
`LEAD(col, n, default)` — value n rows after current in the window; replaces a self-join to the next row
`FIRST_VALUE(col) OVER (...)` — first value in the window; use `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` for predictable behaviour

`LAST_VALUE(col) OVER (...)` — **gotcha:** default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, not through the end. Must specify `ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING` to get the true last value
**Window frames:** `ROWS` counts physical rows (exact); `RANGE` counts value ranges (can include unexpected rows on ties)
Running total: `SUM(col) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
3-period moving avg: `AVG(col) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`
Cumulative sum resets per group: `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)`
days.code:
-- LAG/LEAD: month-over-month sales change
SELECT month, sales,
  LAG(sales, 1, 0)  OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
  LEAD(sales, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next_month,
  sales - LAG(sales, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS mom_change,
  ROUND(100.0 * (sales - LAG(sales,1,0) OVER(ORDER BY month))
        / NULLIF(LAG(sales,1,0) OVER(ORDER BY month), 0), 2) AS mom_pct
FROM monthly_sales;

-- FIRST_VALUE: show each row alongside the first value in its group
SELECT name, dept, salary,
  FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS top_earner_in_dept
FROM employees;

-- LAST_VALUE GOTCHA — must override the default frame
SELECT name, dept, salary,
  LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (
    PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING  -- ← required!
  ) AS lowest_earner_in_dept
FROM employees;

-- Running total
SELECT date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_total
FROM transactions;

-- 7-day moving average
SELECT date, sales,
  AVG(sales) OVER (
    ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM daily_sales;

-- Reset running total per customer
SELECT customer_id, date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_spend
FROM orders;

qa.q: What is the LAST_VALUE gotcha and how do you fix it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The default window frame for LAST_VALUE is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — this means LAST_VALUE only looks from the start of the partition up to the current row, so it returns the current row's own value (not the partition's last value). Fix: explicitly set the frame to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING to make LAST_VALUE look at the entire partition.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: What is the difference between ROWS and RANGE in window frames?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ROWS counts physical rows — ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW always includes exactly 3 rows (or fewer at the start). RANGE counts by value — RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW includes all rows whose ORDER BY value is less than or equal to the current row's value. With ties in the ORDER BY, RANGE can include more rows than expected. ROWS is almost always what you want for moving averages and running totals.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: How would you compute a 12-month moving average of monthly revenue?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SELECT month, revenue, AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS moving_avg_12m FROM monthly_revenue; — ROWS BETWEEN 11 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW gives the current month plus the 11 before it = 12 months total. For months with fewer than 12 data points (at the start), AVG divides by however many rows are actually in the frame.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: How does LAG replace a self-join for consecutive row comparison?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Before window functions, comparing a row to the previous row required a self-join: SELECT a.value - b.value FROM t a JOIN t b ON b.date = DATEADD(DAY,-1,a.date). With LAG: SELECT value - LAG(value,1,value) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS daily_change FROM t. LAG is a single table scan versus a join that can be O(n log n) or worse on large tables.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: How do you calculate a running total that resets per group?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Add PARTITION BY to the window: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_spend. The PARTITION BY customer_id resets the cumulative sum to 0 at the start of each customer's rows. Without PARTITION BY, you get a global running total across all customers.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

days.title: CTEs deep dive — recursive, multiple, CTE vs temp table vs table variable
days.exp: CTEs are fundamental for readable SQL but the performance trade-offs between CTEs, temp tables, and table variables are a genuine senior-level question. Recursive CTEs for hierarchy traversal appear in almost every data engineering interview.
pts: Basic CTE: `WITH cte AS (...)` — named result set scoped to one statement; can reference earlier CTEs in a multi-CTE chain
SQL Server may or may not materialize a CTE — it can inline it like a subquery, meaning multiple references re-execute it multiple times
**Temp table `#temp`:** physically materialized in tempdb; has statistics; can be indexed; persists for the session
**Table variable `@table`:** in-memory by default for small sets; limited statistics; cannot be indexed (except PK); auto-scoped to batch
**When CTE > temp table:** readability, single use, recursive traversal
**When temp table > CTE:** large intermediate result sets that are referenced multiple times in the same query; when statistics matter for optimizer; when you need indexes on the intermediate result
Recursive CTE anatomy: **anchor member** (base case, runs once) `UNION ALL` **recursive member** (references the CTE, runs until no new rows)
`OPTION (MAXRECURSION n)` — default is 100; use 0 for unlimited depth but always have a clear termination condition
Recursive CTE use cases: org charts, bill-of-materials, category trees, date generation, sequence filling
days.code:
-- Multi-CTE: each can reference the previous
WITH dept_avg AS (
  SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM employees GROUP BY dept
),
above_avg AS (
  SELECT e.name, e.salary, e.dept, d.avg_sal
  FROM employees e JOIN dept_avg d ON e.dept = d.dept
  WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal
)
SELECT * FROM above_avg ORDER BY dept, salary DESC;

-- CTE referenced twice = executed twice (unlike a temp table)
WITH expensive AS (SELECT * FROM sales WHERE amount > 10000)
SELECT * FROM expensive e1
JOIN expensive e2 ON e1.customer_id = e2.customer_id AND e1.id != e2.id;
-- expensive is evaluated TWICE above → use #temp for large sets

-- Recursive CTE: org chart
WITH OrgChart AS (
  -- Anchor: root nodes (no manager)
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth,
         CAST(name AS VARCHAR(MAX)) AS path
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  -- Recursive: one level deeper
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.depth + 1,
         oc.path + ' > ' + e.name
  FROM employees e
  JOIN OrgChart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
)
SELECT id, name, depth, path FROM OrgChart
ORDER BY path
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0);

-- Generate date series with recursive CTE
WITH dates AS (
  SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE) AS dt
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DATEADD(DAY, 1, dt) FROM dates WHERE dt < '2024-12-31'
)
SELECT dt FROM dates OPTION (MAXRECURSION 366);

qa.q: What is the performance difference between a CTE referenced multiple times vs a temp table?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A CTE is inlined by SQL Server — if you reference the same CTE twice in a query, it executes twice. A temp table (#temp) is physically materialized in tempdb once: subsequent references read the already-computed result. For a CTE that is large or expensive to compute and is referenced more than once, using a SELECT INTO #temp first and then joining to it twice is significantly faster.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What is the difference between a temp table and a table variable in SQL Server?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Temp table (#temp): physically materialized in tempdb, has statistics (helps the optimizer), can be indexed, visible to nested stored procedures, persists for the session (or until dropped). Table variable (@table): in-memory for small sets, almost no statistics (optimizer assumes 1 row — bad for large sets), no explicit indexes (PK only), scoped to the current batch. Use @table for small sets (< ~100 rows); use #temp for larger intermediate results.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: What are the two required parts of a recursive CTE?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The anchor member (base case): runs exactly once and returns the starting rows — typically WHERE manager_id IS NULL for org charts. The recursive member: references the CTE itself using UNION ALL, runs repeatedly joining the CTE to the underlying table to get one more level of descendants. Recursion stops when the recursive member returns zero new rows. Never use UNION (without ALL) in a recursive CTE — the deduplication check prevents recursion.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What is MAXRECURSION and when do you change it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SQL Server limits recursive CTEs to 100 iterations by default (OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100)) to prevent infinite loops. If your hierarchy or sequence is deeper than 100 levels, you get error 530. Set OPTION (MAXRECURSION 0) for unlimited, but always ensure your recursive member has a clear termination condition (like WHERE dt < '2024-12-31'). Always test that the recursion terminates before removing the default limit.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: When would you use a recursive CTE for date generation?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** To generate a complete calendar table or fill gaps in time-series data without a helper table. The pattern: anchor = SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE), recursive = SELECT DATEADD(DAY,1,dt) WHERE dt < '2024-12-31'. This produces every date in the range. Then LEFT JOIN your data to this date series to find days with no data (gaps). Without a recursive CTE or numbers table, gap-filling requires complex tricks.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

days.title: Classic problems — pivot, unpivot, gaps & islands, string aggregation
days.exp: These patterns combine multiple SQL concepts and test whether you can think set-theoretically about a problem. 'Gaps and islands' is the signature senior-level SQL interview problem — master the key insight (the subtraction trick) and you can solve any variant.
pts: **Gaps in a sequence:** find values missing from a consecutive series; use `ROW_NUMBER() - value` = constant trick or `LAG + DATEDIFF` comparison
**Islands:** consecutive runs of values; key insight: `value - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY value)` is constant within a run; group by this difference
**PIVOT:** rotate rows to columns using `PIVOT(aggregate FOR column IN (val1, val2, ...))` — column list must be static
**Dynamic PIVOT:** generate the column list dynamically using STRING_AGG or FOR XML PATH, then execute with sp_executesql
**String aggregation → rows:** `STRING_SPLIT(string, delimiter)` converts a delimited string to a table of values (SQL Server 2016+)
**Deduplication:** `WITH cte AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM t) DELETE FROM cte WHERE rn > 1`
**Telephone intervals / merging overlapping ranges:** classic advanced problem — requires LAG to detect range starts and running counts
days.code:
-- GAPS: find missing IDs in a sequence
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM items
)
SELECT id - rn AS gap_group_start, MIN(id) AS first_missing
FROM numbered WHERE id != rn  -- id and rn diverge at each gap
GROUP BY id - rn;

-- ISLANDS: find consecutive date ranges
WITH dated AS (
  SELECT login_date,
    DATEADD(DAY, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY login_date), login_date) AS island_key
  FROM logins
)
SELECT MIN(login_date) AS streak_start, MAX(login_date) AS streak_end,
       DATEDIFF(DAY, MIN(login_date), MAX(login_date)) + 1 AS streak_days
FROM dated GROUP BY island_key ORDER BY streak_start;

-- PIVOT: monthly sales per product (static columns)
SELECT product, [Jan], [Feb], [Mar]
FROM (SELECT product, month_name, sales FROM monthly_sales) src
PIVOT (SUM(sales) FOR month_name IN ([Jan],[Feb],[Mar])) pvt;

-- DELETE duplicates, keep lowest id
WITH cte AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn
  FROM users
)
DELETE FROM cte WHERE rn > 1;

-- STRING_SPLIT: expand comma list to rows
SELECT value AS tag FROM STRING_SPLIT('sql,python,java', ',');

-- Merge overlapping date ranges (medical/event scheduling)
WITH range_starts AS (
  SELECT start_date, end_date,
    CASE WHEN start_date <= MAX(end_date) OVER (ORDER BY start_date
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)
    THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS is_new_range
  FROM date_ranges
),
groups AS (SELECT *, SUM(is_new_range) OVER (ORDER BY start_date) AS grp FROM range_starts)
SELECT grp, MIN(start_date) AS merged_start, MAX(end_date) AS merged_end
FROM groups GROUP BY grp;

qa.q: What is the key insight for solving the "islands" problem in SQL?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Within a consecutive sequence, the difference between each value and its ROW_NUMBER() is constant. For the sequence 1,2,3,5,6,9: ROW_NUMBERs are 1,2,3,4,5,6. Differences are 0,0,0,1,1,3. All rows in the same consecutive run share the same difference — that's the "island key." GROUP BY this difference and take MIN/MAX to get each island's start and end.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is the PIVOT operator in SQL Server and what is its limitation?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** PIVOT rotates unique values from one column into multiple columns, applying an aggregate. Syntax: PIVOT(SUM(value) FOR category IN ([A],[B],[C])). The limitation: the column list ([A],[B],[C]) must be hardcoded at query time — you cannot dynamically generate it in standard SQL. For dynamic column lists, you must use dynamic SQL: build the column list with STRING_AGG, construct the full PIVOT query as a string, then execute with sp_executesql.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: How do you efficiently find gaps in a numeric sequence?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use ROW_NUMBER() minus the actual value: WITH cte AS (SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM t) SELECT id-rn AS gap_marker... The id-rn difference increments by 1 at each gap, staying constant within a consecutive run. Alternatively, join the table to a generated number sequence: SELECT n FROM numbers LEFT JOIN t ON t.id = n.n WHERE t.id IS NULL. The recursive CTE date generation pattern also works for specific ranges.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What is STRING_SPLIT and what problems does it solve?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** STRING_SPLIT(string, delimiter) is a table-valued function (SQL Server 2016+) that converts a delimited string into a result set of rows — one row per token. It solves the "comma-separated values in a single column" anti-pattern. Example: for tags = 'sql,python,java', SELECT value FROM STRING_SPLIT(tags, ',') gives three rows. Use it when you need to JOIN or filter on individual items in a delimited string.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: Walk through how you would delete duplicate rows while keeping the row with the lowest ID.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** WITH cte AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id ASC) AS rn FROM users) DELETE FROM cte WHERE rn > 1. ROW_NUMBER() assigns 1 to the row with the lowest id in each duplicate group (ORDER BY id ASC). All subsequent rows in the group get rn = 2, 3, etc. Deleting WHERE rn > 1 removes all duplicates while keeping the first-inserted row.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.
