days.title: Indexing deep dive — covering, filtered, fragmentation, missing index DMVs
days.exp: Index questions at 4 YOE go beyond 'clustered vs non-clustered.' Interviewers expect you to know covering indexes, filtered indexes, when indexes hurt, and how to find missing indexes using DMVs. These come up whenever the interviewer asks 'how would you optimize this query?'
pts: Clustered index: defines the physical sort order of the table (the table IS the B-tree); one per table; lookup is a direct B-tree traversal
Non-clustered index: separate B-tree with key columns + pointer (row locator) to the clustered index or heap; many per table
**Covering index:** an index that includes ALL columns needed by a query (SELECT + WHERE + ORDER BY) — no Key Lookup needed, fastest for read-only queries
**Filtered index:** a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause (e.g., `WHERE status = 'active'`) — smaller, faster, more selective for a subset of data
**Key Lookup:** expensive operation in the execution plan when a non-clustered index is used but the query needs columns not in the index — fix by adding an INCLUDE clause
**INCLUDE clause:** adds non-key columns to the leaf level of a non-clustered index for covering without affecting key order: `CREATE INDEX ix ON orders (status) INCLUDE (amount, date)`
**Index fragmentation:** caused by page splits during inserts/updates. Internal fragmentation (pages not full) → REORGANIZE. External fragmentation (page order out of sequence) → REBUILD.
`sys.dm_db_missing_index_details` / `sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups` — DMVs that track queries the optimizer wanted an index for but none existed
**Index maintenance:** REBUILD (offline, full rewrite) vs REORGANIZE (online, incremental defrag). Rebuild when fragmentation > 30%, Reorganize when 10–30%.
Too many indexes hurt write performance — each INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must update every index on that table
days.code:
-- Covering index: include all columns the query needs
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_status_covering
ON orders (status)
INCLUDE (customer_id, amount, order_date);
-- Now: SELECT customer_id, amount, order_date FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending'
-- uses index-only scan — no Key Lookup

-- Filtered index: only active orders
CREATE INDEX ix_orders_active
ON orders (customer_id, order_date)
WHERE status = 'active';  -- smaller index, faster for active-only queries

-- Check fragmentation
SELECT
  OBJECT_NAME(ips.object_id) AS table_name,
  i.name AS index_name,
  ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent,
  ips.page_count
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'SAMPLED') ips
JOIN sys.indexes i ON ips.object_id = i.object_id AND ips.index_id = i.index_id
WHERE ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent > 10
ORDER BY ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent DESC;

-- Rebuild (offline) when fragmentation > 30%
ALTER INDEX ix_orders_status ON orders REBUILD;

-- Reorganize (online) when fragmentation 10-30%
ALTER INDEX ix_orders_status ON orders REORGANIZE;

-- Missing index recommendations
SELECT
  mid.statement AS table_name,
  mid.equality_columns, mid.inequality_columns, mid.included_columns,
  migs.avg_user_impact,  -- % query improvement estimated
  migs.user_seeks + migs.user_scans AS usage_count
FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_details mid
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups mig ON mid.index_handle = mig.index_handle
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats migs ON mig.index_group_handle = migs.group_handle
ORDER BY migs.avg_user_impact DESC;

qa.q: What is a covering index and how does it eliminate Key Lookups?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A covering index contains all the columns a specific query needs — the WHERE clause key columns plus all columns in the SELECT list and ORDER BY. When a query can be satisfied entirely from the index, the optimizer performs an index-only scan without going back to the base table (no Key Lookup). You create one by adding an INCLUDE clause: CREATE INDEX ix ON orders (status) INCLUDE (amount, date) — status is the key, amount and date are stored at the leaf level for covering.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: What is a filtered index and when would you use one?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A filtered index is a non-clustered index with a WHERE clause that limits which rows are included. Example: CREATE INDEX ix_orders_pending ON orders (customer_id) WHERE status = 'pending'. This creates a small, highly selective index covering only pending orders. Benefits: smaller size, faster reads for the filtered subset, less write overhead than a full index. Use when a large table has a frequently-queried subset (active records, non-null values, specific status).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: What is the difference between REBUILD and REORGANIZE for index maintenance?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** REBUILD drops and recreates the index — removes both internal and external fragmentation, updates statistics, but is an offline operation by default (blocks reads/writes) unless WITH ONLINE = ON (Enterprise edition). REORGANIZE physically reorders the leaf pages in-place — removes external fragmentation, cannot remove internal fragmentation, always online, slower for high-fragmentation cases. Rule of thumb: REORGANIZE for fragmentation 10-30%, REBUILD for > 30%.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: How do you find missing indexes in SQL Server?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Query sys.dm_db_missing_index_details joined with sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats. These DMVs track every time the query optimizer wanted an index that didn't exist, including the equality columns, inequality columns, and include columns it would have wanted. The avg_user_impact column shows the estimated % improvement. Warning: treat these as suggestions, not commands — creating every suggested index harms write performance.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: Why do too many indexes hurt performance?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Every INSERT must add a row to every non-clustered index on that table. Every UPDATE to indexed columns must update those indexes. Every DELETE must remove the row from every index. A table with 10 non-clustered indexes effectively writes to 11 places (base + 10 indexes) for every INSERT. This is why OLTP tables should have fewer, carefully chosen indexes, and OLAP/reporting tables (fewer writes) can have more.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

days.title: Transactions, isolation levels, deadlocks — complete deep dive
days.exp: ACID properties and isolation levels are asked in almost every senior .NET+SQL interview — partly because they connect directly to how you write safe application code. Know each isolation level's anomalies by name. The READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT distinction from READ COMMITTED is a real differentiator.
pts: **ACID:** Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state before/after), Isolation (no partial changes visible), Durability (committed = on disk)
**READ UNCOMMITTED:** dirty reads possible (can read rows another transaction has modified but not committed). Fastest, least safe. Use `WITH (NOLOCK)` hint.
**READ COMMITTED (default):** no dirty reads; but non-repeatable reads possible (same row can change between two reads in one transaction)
**REPEATABLE READ:** no dirty reads or non-repeatable reads; but phantom reads possible (new rows can appear between two queries with the same WHERE)
**SERIALIZABLE:** no anomalies; fully isolated but maximum blocking — range locks prevent phantom reads

**READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI):** SQL Server extension — uses row versioning in tempdb; readers never block writers; no dirty reads; enable at database level (`ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON`)
**SNAPSHOT isolation:** each transaction sees a snapshot of data from when the transaction began; detects write conflicts; must be enabled per database
**Deadlock:** two transactions each holding a lock the other needs — circular wait. SQL Server auto-detects and kills the "deadlock victim" (error 1205).
**Deadlock prevention:** always acquire locks in the same order across all code paths; keep transactions short; use RCSI to reduce lock contention
**Deadlock detection:** deadlock graph logged to SQL Server error log and Extended Events; shows the two transactions and their conflicting resources

qa.q: What are the four isolation levels and what anomaly does each prevent?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** READ UNCOMMITTED: prevents nothing — dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads all possible. READ COMMITTED (default): prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ: prevents dirty reads and non-repeatable reads (same row can't change within a transaction). SERIALIZABLE: prevents all three — dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads (new rows matching a WHERE can't appear). Higher isolation = more correctness, more blocking.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

qa.q: What is the difference between READ COMMITTED and READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Both prevent dirty reads. Standard READ COMMITTED uses shared locks — a reader blocks a writer and vice versa. READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI) uses row versioning: instead of taking a shared lock, a reader reads a committed snapshot of the row from tempdb. Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. RCSI provides better concurrency with the same consistency guarantees. Enable at the database level: ALTER DATABASE YourDB SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

qa.q: What causes a deadlock and how do you prevent it in a .NET application?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A deadlock occurs when Transaction A holds Lock X and waits for Lock Y, while Transaction B holds Lock Y and waits for Lock X — circular wait. SQL Server detects and kills the victim (error 1205). Prevention in .NET: (1) always access tables in the same order across all code paths, (2) keep transactions as short as possible, (3) enable RCSI to reduce lock contention, (4) retry logic in .NET code for error 1205 — catch SqlException where Number == 1205 and retry after a brief delay.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

qa.q: What is SNAPSHOT isolation and how does it differ from RCSI?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Both use row versioning. RCSI enables row versioning for the default READ COMMITTED level at the database level — all readers automatically get this behaviour. SNAPSHOT isolation is an explicit transaction-level setting: each transaction sees a point-in-time snapshot of the database from when the transaction began. SNAPSHOT detects write conflicts (throws an error if two transactions update the same row). RCSI does not detect conflicts — last writer wins. Use SNAPSHOT for long-running read transactions that need a consistent view.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

qa.q: What is the WITH (NOLOCK) hint and when should you use it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** WITH (NOLOCK) is equivalent to READ UNCOMMITTED at the table level — it reads rows without acquiring shared locks, including rows in the middle of an uncommitted transaction (dirty reads). Use it only for approximate counts or dashboards where slightly stale or inconsistent data is acceptable (e.g., a row count for a large table). Never use WITH (NOLOCK) for financial calculations, integrity-critical reads, or any query where reading uncommitted data would cause incorrect results.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

days.title: Advanced features — MERGE, OUTPUT, JSON, dynamic SQL, stored procedures
days.exp: MERGE (upsert), OUTPUT (capture changes), and JSON functions are real-world T-SQL features that appear in senior SQL interviews and the kind of compliance/integration work you're already doing. Dynamic SQL is asked for its risks and safe patterns.
pts: **MERGE:** combines INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into a single statement based on a match condition — classic upsert pattern. Use carefully: known edge cases with duplicate matches in source.
**OUTPUT clause:** captures the rows affected by INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE into a result set or table variable — useful for audit trails, returning IDs of inserted rows, or capturing before/after values

**JSON in SQL Server:** `FOR JSON PATH` / `FOR JSON AUTO` — serialize query results to JSON; `JSON_VALUE(col, '$.key')` — extract a scalar; `JSON_QUERY(col, '$.array')` — extract an object/array; `OPENJSON(col)` — parse JSON into rows
**Dynamic SQL:** build and execute SQL strings at runtime using `sp_executesql @sql, @params, @val`; use parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection
**SQL injection risk:** NEVER concatenate user input directly into a SQL string. Use sp_executesql with typed parameters.
Stored procedures: compiled, can have input/output parameters, support transactions, reduce network round-trips; trade-off: business logic in DB vs application layer
Temp tables (#) in stored procedures reset on each execution; table variables (@) go out of scope at end of batch

qa.q: What is the MERGE statement and what is its main gotcha?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** MERGE combines INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE into a single statement based on a match condition between a target table and a source. It's the SQL upsert operator. The main gotcha: if the source has duplicate rows matching the same target row, the MERGE raises an error. Always de-duplicate the source first: WITH deduped AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn FROM source) ... SELECT * FROM deduped WHERE rn = 1.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: What does the OUTPUT clause do and give two practical use cases?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** OUTPUT captures the rows affected by a data modification (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and returns them as a result set or inserts them into a table. Use case 1: get the auto-generated IDs after a bulk INSERT without a separate SELECT. Use case 2: audit trail — UPDATE employees SET salary = salary*1.1 OUTPUT DELETED.salary AS before, INSERTED.salary AS after INTO salary_audit — captures before and after values in a single statement.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What are the JSON functions in SQL Server and when do you use each?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** FOR JSON PATH/AUTO: serialize query results to a JSON string — use when your API or client expects JSON. JSON_VALUE(col, '$.key'): extract a single scalar value from a JSON column — use for filtering or selecting individual fields. JSON_QUERY(col, '$.nested'): extract a JSON object or array (not a scalar) — preserves JSON structure. OPENJSON(col): parse a JSON string into a table of rows — use when you receive JSON documents and need to query them relationally. ISJSON(col): validate whether a string is valid JSON.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is SQL injection and how does sp_executesql prevent it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SQL injection is when user-supplied input is concatenated into a SQL string and executed as code. If a user inputs '; DROP TABLE users; -- as a parameter, string concatenation executes the DROP. sp_executesql with parameters prevents this: the parameter value is passed separately and treated as data, never as SQL code, regardless of its content. Always use sp_executesql @sql, @params_definition, @param = @value pattern for dynamic SQL with user input.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What are the trade-offs of putting business logic in stored procedures vs the application layer?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Stored procedures: compiled execution plan, reduced network round-trips, enforced schema, centralised logic. Trade-offs: harder to version control and test, tightly coupled to the database, requires DBA permissions for changes. Application layer: easier to test, version control, and deploy independently; uses familiar .NET/ORM patterns; but requires more network round-trips and loses SQL Server compilation benefits. Most modern teams prefer application-layer logic (using EF Core or Dapper) and reserve stored procedures for performance-critical or DBA-managed operations.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

days.title: Performance tuning, execution plans, parameter sniffing, full mock
days.exp: Performance tuning at 4 YOE means being able to read an execution plan, explain parameter sniffing, and suggest concrete fixes. These questions appear whenever the interviewer asks 'this query is slow — what would you do?'
pts: **Execution plan operators to know:** Table Scan (no usable index), Index Scan (index exists but reads all rows), Index Seek (selective filter uses the index), Key Lookup (extra trip to the base table for non-covered columns), Hash Join (large inputs), Nested Loop (small/indexed inputs)
**Cost percentage in the plan:** an operator with 80% cost is your bottleneck — focus optimisation there

**Parameter sniffing:** SQL Server compiles a stored procedure with the first parameter values it sees, reuses that plan for all subsequent calls. If later calls have very different parameters (high vs low cardinality), the cached plan may be suboptimal.

**Fix parameter sniffing:** `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` forces recompile per execution (use for queries with wildly varying parameters). `WITH RECOMPILE` on the stored proc (always recompiles — use sparingly). Local variables (capture parameter into a local variable — breaks sniffing but also loses the first-call optimisation).
**OPTION (MAXDOP n):** limits degree of parallelism for a specific query
**Query Store:** tracks query plans and performance over time; lets you force a specific plan; available in SQL Server 2016+
**Statistics:** the optimizer uses statistics to estimate row counts. Outdated statistics cause bad plans. `UPDATE STATISTICS table` or `sp_updatestats` refreshes them.
Always measure with SET STATISTICS TIME ON and SET STATISTICS IO ON before and after any optimisation change
days.code:
-- Read execution plan
-- In SSMS: Query → Include Actual Execution Plan
-- Look for: Table Scan (bad), Key Lookup (add INCLUDE), high-cost nodes

-- Enable I/O and time stats
SET STATISTICS IO ON;
SET STATISTICS TIME ON;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
-- Output: logical reads = 1200 → consider an index on customer_id

-- Parameter sniffing: stored proc compiled for rare case, bad for common case
CREATE PROCEDURE GetOrders @status NVARCHAR(20)
AS
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = @status;
-- First call: @status = 'cancelled' (few rows → nested loop plan compiled)
-- Later calls: @status = 'pending' (millions of rows → needs hash join, but gets nested loop)

-- Fix 1: OPTION (RECOMPILE)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = @status OPTION (RECOMPILE);

-- Fix 2: local variable to break sniffing
DECLARE @local_status NVARCHAR(20) = @status;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = @local_status;

-- Query Store: view top queries by CPU
SELECT TOP 10
  qsq.query_id,
  SUBSTRING(qsqt.query_sql_text, 1, 100) AS query_text,
  qsrs.avg_cpu_time, qsrs.avg_logical_io_reads
FROM sys.query_store_query qsq
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qsqt ON qsq.query_text_id = qsqt.query_text_id
JOIN sys.query_store_plan qsp ON qsq.query_id = qsp.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_runtime_stats qsrs ON qsp.plan_id = qsrs.plan_id
ORDER BY qsrs.avg_cpu_time DESC;

-- Force a specific plan via Query Store
EXEC sp_query_store_force_plan @query_id = 12, @plan_id = 3;

qa.q: What is parameter sniffing and when is it a problem?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Parameter sniffing is SQL Server's behaviour of compiling a stored procedure's execution plan using the first parameter values it encounters, then reusing that plan for all subsequent calls. It's a problem when parameter values have wildly different cardinalities: a plan compiled for @status = 'cancelled' (100 rows → nested loop) is a terrible plan for @status = 'pending' (10 million rows → should be hash join). The cached plan causes dramatically poor performance for the high-cardinality case.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What are the three ways to fix parameter sniffing?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1) OPTION (RECOMPILE) hint on the query: forces recompilation on every execution using the actual parameter values — best when execution frequency is low or parameter variance is extreme. 2) WITH RECOMPILE on the stored procedure: always recompiles — use when every parameter variation needs a fresh plan but execution frequency is manageable. 3) Local variables: DECLARE @local = @param; SELECT ... WHERE col = @local — SQL Server can't sniff local variables so it uses a generic plan (may not be optimal but is consistent).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What execution plan operators indicate performance problems?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Table Scan: no usable index — add an index on the filter column. Index Scan: index exists but reads all rows — either the filter is not selective enough, or wrong index. Key Lookup: non-clustered index doesn't cover all needed columns — add INCLUDE clause. Hash Spill to disk: insufficient memory for the hash join — reduce parallelism or fix statistics. Parallelism (arrows on operators): sometimes queries use unnecessary parallelism — add OPTION (MAXDOP 1) for OLTP queries that shouldn't parallelize.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: What is the Query Store in SQL Server 2016+ and what problem does it solve?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Query Store automatically captures query text, execution plans, and runtime statistics over time — essentially a flight recorder for SQL Server. It solves the "plan regression" problem: when a new plan is adopted after a statistics update or index change and performs worse, Query Store lets you identify the regression and force the old plan with sp_query_store_force_plan. It also shows the top CPU, I/O, and duration consumers to prioritise optimisation work.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: What is the difference between SET STATISTICS IO and SET STATISTICS TIME?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SET STATISTICS IO ON outputs the number of logical reads (reads from the buffer cache) and physical reads (reads from disk) for each table in the query. Logical reads are your primary measure of query efficiency — fewer reads = better plan. SET STATISTICS TIME ON outputs the CPU time and elapsed time for query compilation and execution. Use both together before and after any optimisation change to measure concrete improvement rather than relying on perceived speed.

days.title: Gotchas everyone forgets -- the traps that pass code review but break production
days.exp: These are not obscure edge cases -- they're the specific mistakes that even experienced developers make under interview pressure or late-Friday deploys, because the wrong version LOOKS correct and often works fine on small test data. Drill this day right before any interview; it is the highest density of 'wait, I do that wrong' per minute in the whole plan.
pts: **COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column):** COUNT(*) counts every row including NULLs. COUNT(column) skips NULLs in that column. Silently different results on the same table if any column has NULLs -- always ask 'am I counting rows or non-null values?'

**LEFT JOIN + WHERE on the right table = silent INNER JOIN:** `WHERE o.status = 'active'` after a LEFT JOIN drops every row where o.status is NULL (no match) -- because NULL = 'active' is never true. Move the condition into the ON clause to preserve the outer join.
**NULL = NULL is NULL, not TRUE:** `WHERE col = NULL` returns zero rows, always, silently. Must use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL. This single fact explains half of all NULL-related SQL bugs.

**NOT IN poisoned by a single NULL:** if the subquery in `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT ...)` returns even one NULL, the entire NOT IN returns zero rows for every outer row -- not an error, just silently wrong. NOT EXISTS does not have this problem.

**WHERE cannot use aggregates, HAVING can:** `WHERE COUNT(*) > 5` is a syntax error because WHERE runs before GROUP BY in the logical execution order. This trips people who haven't internalized FROM->WHERE->GROUP BY->HAVING->SELECT->ORDER BY.

**RANK() vs DENSE_RANK() gap after ties:** two rows tied at rank 1 -> RANK() jumps to 3 for the next row, DENSE_RANK() goes to 2. A 'find the 2nd highest' query using RANK() silently returns nothing when there's a tie at 1st, because rank 2 never gets assigned.

**GROUP BY column must cover every non-aggregated SELECT column:** selecting a column that's neither in GROUP BY nor wrapped in an aggregate is a hard error in SQL Server/Postgres, but returns an arbitrary unpredictable value in older MySQL -- a silent bug that only appears when porting queries between database engines.

**UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE:** the single most catastrophic SQL mistake -- always write and verify the WHERE clause (or run the equivalent SELECT first) before running an UPDATE or DELETE, especially in a shared or production environment.
**BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends:** `WHERE amount BETWEEN 100 AND 200` includes both 100 and 200. Off-by-one bugs happen when someone assumes it behaves like a half-open range.

**Implicit type conversion silently breaks index usage:** comparing a VARCHAR column to an unquoted number, or an INT column to a quoted string, can force SQL Server to convert every row before comparing -- turning a fast index seek into a full table scan with no error, just unexplained slowness.
days.code:
-- COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) -- different answers, same table
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_rows, COUNT(email) AS rows_with_email
FROM customers;
-- If 2 of 10 customers have NULL email: total_rows=10, rows_with_email=8

-- LEFT JOIN trap
SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'active';              -- ❌ drops customers with NO orders at all

SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id AND o.status = 'active';  -- ✓ correct

-- NOT IN poisoned by NULL
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);  -- ❌ returns NOTHING if any customer_id is NULL

SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);  -- ✓ safe

-- RANK vs DENSE_RANK on a tie
-- Salaries: 100, 100, 90, 80
SELECT salary,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,   -- 1, 1, 3, 4  (no rank 2!)
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk    -- 1, 1, 2, 3  (rank 2 exists)
FROM employees;

-- The classic catastrophic mistake -- ALWAYS check WHERE before running
-- DELETE FROM orders;                    -- ❌ deletes EVERY row, no confirmation
-- DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 42;       -- ✓ run the SELECT version first to verify

-- Implicit conversion silently kills an index
-- If order_id is VARCHAR but compared to an unquoted number:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = 12345;      -- ❌ may force a full scan
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = '12345';    -- ✓ matches the column's actual type

qa.q: Why does COUNT(*) sometimes give a different answer than COUNT(some_column) on the exact same query?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of content. COUNT(column) only counts rows where that specific column is NOT NULL. If a table has rows with NULL values in that column, COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) diverge -- and this is not a bug, it's the defined behavior, which is exactly why it's a common source of 'why do these two numbers not match' confusion.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What silently breaks when you add a WHERE clause on a right-table column after a LEFT JOIN?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** It converts the LEFT JOIN into an effective INNER JOIN, because any row where the right table had no match has NULL in that column, and NULL never equals anything in a WHERE comparison -- so those rows get filtered out along with the genuinely non-matching ones. The intended 'keep rows even with no match' behavior of LEFT JOIN is destroyed. Fix: move the condition into the ON clause instead of WHERE.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: Why does 'WHERE id NOT IN (subquery)' sometimes return zero rows even when it obviously shouldn't?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If the subquery's result set contains even a single NULL value, NOT IN returns UNKNOWN (not TRUE) for every comparison due to SQL's three-valued logic -- meaning the entire outer WHERE clause evaluates to nothing matching, for every row, silently. There's no error message; it just returns an empty result set. NOT EXISTS doesn't have this failure mode because it checks for row absence rather than comparing against a list of values.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: Why can't you write WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 in SQL, and what should you write instead?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The logical execution order of a SQL query is FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY. WHERE executes before GROUP BY has run, so no aggregate values exist yet for WHERE to filter on -- it's a syntax error, not just bad practice. HAVING runs after GROUP BY specifically so it can filter on aggregate results: HAVING COUNT(*) > 5.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: Someone asks for the '2nd highest salary' using RANK() and gets zero rows even though the data clearly has more than one salary value. What happened?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If the highest salary is shared by two or more employees (a tie), RANK() assigns both of them rank 1, then skips directly to rank 3 for the next distinct value -- rank 2 never gets assigned to any row. A query filtering WHERE rnk = 2 finds nothing. DENSE_RANK() doesn't have this gap -- ties still share a rank, but the next distinct value gets the very next consecutive rank number, so 'Nth highest' queries should default to DENSE_RANK() unless there's a specific reason not to.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

days.title: Advanced Window Functions & Analytical SQL
days.exp: Senior SQL interviews test window framing (ROWS/RANGE BETWEEN), analytical functions like QUALIFY, PERCENTILE_CONT, and CUME_DIST.
pts: **ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW** vs **RANGE** (RANGE evaluates duplicates as single frame boundary).
**PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency)** for continuous median calculation across millions of rows.
**CUME_DIST()** (cumulative distribution percentage) vs **PERCENT_RANK()**.
Filtering window function outputs efficiently without wrapping everything in nested CTEs.
days.code:
SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id
    ORDER BY order_date
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  ) AS moving_avg_3_orders
FROM Orders;

qa.q: What is the key performance difference between ROWS and RANGE in SQL window functions?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ROWS operates on physical row offsets and is fast/memory-efficient. RANGE operates on logical values, requiring SQL Server to sort and aggregate duplicate values together, which often causes costly tempdb spills for large datasets.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Provides high readability and single-pass analytical aggregation, but can increase RAM grants compared to traditional indexed grouping.

qa.q: How do you compute the 95th percentile latency per API endpoint in T-SQL?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use PERCENTILE_CONT(0.95) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY duration_ms) OVER (PARTITION BY endpoint_path).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Window functions operate on a set of rows defined by the OVER() clause without collapsing them into a single row, allocating memory segments for frame calculation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Partitioning over non-indexed columns with huge row counts forces expensive Sort operators and TempDB spills in execution plans.

days.title: Query Execution Plan Deep-Dive & Parameter Sniffing
days.exp: Diagnosing production SQL slowness requires reading execution plans, catching parameter sniffing, implicit conversions, and memory grant issues.
pts: **Parameter Sniffing:** SQL Server compiles a plan based on the first parameter passed; bad for skewed data distributions.
**Mitigations:** `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`, `OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@var = value))`, local variable assignment, Query Store hints.
**Implicit Conversions:** passing `VARCHAR` to `NVARCHAR` indexed column causes index scan instead of index seek.
**Memory Grant Warnings:** `RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE` waits when hash joins/sorts request excessive memory allocations.
days.code:
-- Fix parameter sniffing for skewed tenant data:
SELECT * FROM TenantLogs WITH (NOLOCK)
WHERE TenantId = @TenantId
OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@TenantId = 1001));

qa.q: What causes parameter sniffing and what are three ways to solve it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Parameter sniffing happens when SQL Server reuses an execution plan compiled for an unusual initial parameter value. Solutions: 1. OPTION (RECOMPILE) for infrequent queries with high parameter variance. 2. OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR ...) for known average values. 3. Copying parameters to local variables inside stored procedures.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: Why does an implicit datatype conversion destroy index seek performance?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If an indexed column is VARCHAR(50) but the query parameter is passed as NVARCHAR(50), SQL Server must apply the CONVERT() function to every row in the column before comparing, converting an index seek into an index scan.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

days.title: Columnstore Indexes & TempDB Optimization
days.exp: Modern data platform interviews cover Columnstore for analytical queries and TempDB bottleneck resolution.
pts: **Clustered Columnstore Indexes (CCI):** compressed columnar storage, segment elimination, batch mode execution for analytics.
**Non-clustered Columnstore Indexes (NCCI):** added onto transactional OLTP tables for real-time operational analytics (HTAP).
**TempDB Contention:** `PAGELATCH_UP` / `PAGELATCH_EX` on allocation maps (PFS/GAM/SGAM) under high concurrency.
**Table Variables vs Temp Tables (`#tbl`):** `#tbl` has statistics and supports indexes; table variables lack column statistics (estimated 1 row).
days.code:
CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX CCI_FactSales ON FactSales;
-- Enables batch mode processing and 10x-50x compression ratio

qa.q: When should you use Columnstore indexes instead of B-Tree indexes?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use Columnstore for data warehousing, analytical queries scanning millions of rows, and aggregations (SUM, AVG). Columnstore uses column-based compression and batch mode execution. Stick to B-Tree indexes for OLTP workloads doing point lookups and single-row updates.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Indexes store data in B-Tree structures. Clustered indexes dictate physical row storage on disk leaf pages; non-clustered indexes point to clustered keys or RIDs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Over-indexing degrades write performance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations and leads to index fragmentation and page splits.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Covering indexes eliminate costly Key Lookups for read-heavy workloads but increase storage footprint and write transaction overhead.

qa.q: Why can Table Variables cause terrible performance for large datasets compared to Temp Tables?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Table Variables do not maintain column statistics. The query optimizer assumes a table variable has 1 row regardless of actual size, frequently choosing nested loop joins instead of hash joins and under-allocating memory.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

days.title: C# OOP & SOLID — be precise, not encyclopaedic
days.exp: OOP questions at 4 YOE are not "define polymorphism." They're "show me you understand virtual/override vs new, and give me a real SOLID example from your own code."
pts: **Abstract class:** can have state (fields), constructors, and partial implementation. Use when sharing code within a related class family
**Interface:** pure contract. C# 8+ allows default method implementations, but no instance fields. Use for capabilities across unrelated types
**`virtual`/`override`:** true polymorphism — even accessed via a base reference, the derived method is called (runtime dispatch via vtable)
**`new` (hiding):** derived method only called if accessed via derived-type reference. Via base reference → base method runs (compile-time)
**SOLID:** for each principle, have ONE concrete example from your work (evidence pipeline = Open/Closed; injectable providers = Dependency Inversion)

qa.q: What is the difference between virtual/override and new (method hiding) in C#?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** virtual/override uses runtime polymorphism — C# looks up the actual runtime type and calls the override, even through a base-class reference. new (hiding) is compile-time — calling through a base reference invokes the base method, not the derived one. Hiding breaks Liskov Substitution and is usually a design smell.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Explicit scoping ensures request isolation, but requires IServiceScopeFactory for background hosted services.

qa.q: When would you choose abstract class over interface?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use abstract class when: you need to share state (fields) or concrete implementation, you need a constructor, or subclasses are closely related and share a common identity. Use interface when multiple unrelated types need the same capability, or when implementing multiple "contracts" (C# doesn't support multiple abstract class inheritance).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

**Elevator Pitch:** In ComplySec360's evidence pipeline: the core orchestration engine is closed for modification. Adding a new integration means creating a new IEvidenceProvider implementation — not editing the engine. The SCIM provisioning system follows the same pattern: each IdP is a separate IProvisioningStrategy without touching the provisioning core.

days.title: LINQ, delegates, async/await, generics
days.exp: These four are grouped together because they test whether you really understand C# beyond syntax. The most common trip-ups: forgetting LINQ is deferred, and using async void.
pts: **Deferred LINQ:** `IEnumerable<T>` query doesn't execute until enumerated. Calling `.Count()` twice hits the DB twice. Use `.ToList()` to materialize once
**`Select`:** 1:1 projection. **`SelectMany`:** flattens one level (list-of-lists → flat list)
**Delegates → Events:** events wrap delegates to prevent external invocation/overwriting of the invocation list
**`async void` is dangerous:** exceptions propagate to SynchronizationContext and crash the process — never catchable by caller. Always use `async Task`
**`ConfigureAwait(false)`:** don't capture SynchronizationContext — use in library/infrastructure code to avoid deadlocks
**Generics constraints:** `where T : class, new()`. Covariance: `out T` (`IEnumerable<Dog>` where `IEnumerable<Animal>` expected). Contravariance: `in T`

qa.q: What is deferred execution in LINQ and what is the practical risk?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A LINQ query on IEnumerable/IQueryable doesn't execute until you iterate it. The risk: enumerate the same query twice and you hit the database twice. Fix: call .ToList() once to materialize into memory, then work with the list.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is the difference between Task, Task<T>, and ValueTask<T>?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Task = async operation with no return value. Task<T> = async operation returning T. ValueTask<T> is a struct (no heap allocation) for methods that often complete synchronously — like cache hits. Only use ValueTask when profiling shows Task allocation is a measurable bottleneck.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** C# compiler synthesizes an IAsyncStateMachine struct. Awaiting incomplete tasks yields control to the caller; thread pool threads resume via TaskScheduler/SynchronizationContext.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Blocking async code with .Result or .Wait() on single-threaded synchronization contexts leads to deadlocks and thread pool starvation.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async preserves thread pool scalability for I/O operations, but introduces state machine allocations and complex exception bubbling.

qa.q: What is ConfigureAwait(false) and when should you use it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** By default, awaiting captures the SynchronizationContext and resumes on it (important for UI threads). ConfigureAwait(false) says "resume on any thread pool thread." Use it in library/infrastructure code to avoid deadlocks in calling code that uses .Result or .Wait() on async methods.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** C# compiler synthesizes an IAsyncStateMachine struct. Awaiting incomplete tasks yields control to the caller; thread pool threads resume via TaskScheduler/SynchronizationContext.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Blocking async code with .Result or .Wait() on single-threaded synchronization contexts leads to deadlocks and thread pool starvation.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async preserves thread pool scalability for I/O operations, but introduces state machine allocations and complex exception bubbling.

days.title: C# 14 / .NET 10 — what's actually new
days.exp: C# 14 ships with .NET 10 (Nov 2025, current LTS). The theme is reducing boilerplate. Three features matter most for interviews: field keyword, extension members, null-conditional assignment.
pts: **`field` keyword:** custom property get/set without a separate backing field — `field` refers to the auto-generated backing field inside the accessor
**Extension members:** C# 14 extends the extension concept to properties, operators, and static members via `extension(Type x) { }` blocks
**Null-conditional assignment:** `customer?.Address = newAddress;` is now valid — no-op if customer is null
**First-class `Span<T>`:** new implicit conversions between Span, ReadOnlySpan, and arrays — performance story
**Partial constructors & events:** `partial` extended to constructors and events (useful with source generators)
**`nameof` on unbound generics:** `nameof(List<>)` now works — minor but signals you read release notes

qa.q: What problem does the C# 14 field keyword solve?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** It eliminates the need to declare a separate private backing field for properties with custom get/set logic. Before C# 14, you needed a private _myField just to add null-checking in the setter. With field, you write the logic directly in the accessor and field refers to the auto-generated backing field.

qa.q: What is new about extension members in C# 14?

days.title: ASP.NET Core — middleware, DI lifetimes, Minimal APIs
days.exp: The middleware pipeline and DI lifetimes are the two most-asked ASP.NET Core concepts. The captive dependency trap is a classic interview gotcha — know not just that it's wrong but exactly what breaks.
pts: **Middleware pipeline:** request flows in registration order, response flows back in reverse. Order is critical
**DI Lifetimes:** Transient = new instance every resolution, Scoped = one per HTTP request, Singleton = one for app lifetime
**Captive dependency:** Scoped inside Singleton — the Scoped service is created once and held forever, breaking per-request isolation. ASP.NET Core throws in development mode
**Minimal APIs vs Controllers:** Minimal = less ceremony, great for microservices. Controllers = better for large APIs (filters, model binding conventions, organized routing)
**Action Filters vs Middleware:** Middleware applies to all requests. Action Filters are MVC-specific, apply to controller/action scope

qa.q: What is the middleware pipeline and why does order matter?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Middleware components form a chain — each calls next() to pass the request forward, or short-circuits by returning directly. Order matters because each middleware only "sees" what has been set up before it. Authentication must run before Authorization so the identity is established when the auth check runs. Exception handling must be first to wrap everything else.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Explicit scoping ensures request isolation, but requires IServiceScopeFactory for background hosted services.

qa.q: What is a captive dependency and what breaks?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A captive dependency is when a Singleton service holds a reference to a Scoped service. The Scoped service is meant to be created fresh per HTTP request. Captured inside a Singleton, it lives as long as the Singleton — across all requests. It can hold stale state or a disposed DbContext. ASP.NET Core throws InvalidOperationException in development when it detects this pattern.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Explicit scoping ensures request isolation, but requires IServiceScopeFactory for background hosted services.

qa.q: When would you choose Minimal APIs over controller-based APIs?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Minimal APIs for: microservices with a small number of focused endpoints, serverless/cloud functions where cold start matters, prototyping. Controllers for: larger APIs with complex model binding, action filters, organized routing, and teams already familiar with MVC conventions. For your SCIM provisioning project, minimal APIs are a natural fit — the API surface is small and well-defined.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

days.title: EF Core — change tracking, N+1, migrations, EF Core 10
days.exp: EF Core questions at 4 YOE are almost never "how do you add a migration." They're "explain how change tracking works" and "what is the N+1 problem." These connect directly to your production work.
pts: **Change tracking:** EF monitors all queried entities by default, comparing snapshots on `SaveChanges()`. Only modified properties generate SQL
**`AsNoTracking()`:** disables change tracking — typically 20–40% faster for read-only queries
**N+1 problem:** load N entities, access navigation property in a loop → 1+N database round-trips. Fix: `.Include(o => o.Customer)`
**EF Core 10 — named query filters:** multiple `HasQueryFilter()` per entity type, selectively disable individual filters
**EF Core 10 — native JSON columns:** model JSON columns directly without manual serialization — great for metadata in a compliance platform
`DbContext` is already a Unit of Work — `SaveChanges()` flushes all changes in one transaction

qa.q: What is the N+1 problem in EF Core and how do you fix it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** N+1 happens when you load N entities and then access a navigation property on each in a loop — triggering 1 additional query per entity (total: 1 + N queries). Fix with .Include(e => e.RelatedEntity) to eagerly load in a single JOIN query. Detect it by enabling EF Core query logging — you'll see the same query repeated N times.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

qa.q: When should you use AsNoTracking()?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** For read-only queries where you won't call SaveChanges() on the retrieved entities — API responses, reports, exports. EF Core skips creating change-tracking snapshots, reducing memory usage and processing time by typically 20–40%. Never use it if you need to update those entities afterward.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Garbage Collector uses generational collection (Gen 0, 1, 2, LOH, POH) with mark-sweep-compact phases. Span<T> provides stack-allocated contiguous representation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Excessive allocations of large objects (>85KB) trigger frequent Gen 2 / LOH collections, causing GC pause spikes and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> and Memory<T> eliminate heap allocations and copy costs, but ref structs cannot be boxed or captured in async state machines.

qa.q: How does EF Core's DbContext relate to the Repository and Unit of Work patterns?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** DbContext already implements both. It's a Unit of Work because SaveChanges() flushes all pending changes in a single transaction. It's a Repository because DbSet<T> provides query, add, update, and delete operations. Adding an extra Repository wrapper usually just adds indirection without benefit — unless you need to support multiple ORMs or deep unit-test isolation.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

days.title: Architecture, patterns, GC, deadlocks — review
days.exp: Day 7 consolidates architecture-level thinking. At 4 YOE, interviewers expect you to have opinions — not just know that patterns exist, but know when they're worth the trade-off.
pts: **Repository + UoW:** if you're using EF Core, you already have both. Extra wrapper is usually over-engineering unless you need to swap ORMs
**IoC vs DI:** Inversion of Control is the principle (depend on abstractions). Dependency Injection is one implementation pattern (inject dependencies rather than creating them internally)
**GC generations:** Gen 0 (new, cheapest, most frequent), Gen 1 (survived Gen 0), Gen 2 (long-lived, LOH). Short-lived allocations in .NET are essentially free

**SQL vs threading deadlock:** SQL = two transactions waiting for each other's row locks (SQL Server detects and kills victim). Threading = two threads waiting for each other's Monitor locks (no auto-detection)
**STAR stories:** prepare Situation→Task→Action→Result for BMS migration, Zintara AI platform, ComplySec360 evidence pipeline

qa.q: Should you wrap EF Core's DbContext in a Repository + Unit of Work layer?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** In most cases: no. DbContext already provides both patterns. Wrapping adds boilerplate, loses EF-specific features like .Include and .AsSplitQuery, and the "testability" argument is better addressed with EF Core's in-memory provider. Valid exceptions: if you genuinely need to support multiple data stores, or if the domain model must be completely decoupled from the ORM.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

qa.q: What is the difference between Gen 0, Gen 1, and Gen 2 garbage collection?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Gen 0 is the nursery — all new allocations go here. GC is fast (milliseconds) and frequent because it scans only a small portion of the heap. Objects surviving a Gen 0 collection are promoted to Gen 1, then Gen 2. Gen 2 GC is slower and rarer. The key insight: .NET is optimized for short-lived allocations — creating and discarding many small objects is fine.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Garbage Collector uses generational collection (Gen 0, 1, 2, LOH, POH) with mark-sweep-compact phases. Span<T> provides stack-allocated contiguous representation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Excessive allocations of large objects (>85KB) trigger frequent Gen 2 / LOH collections, causing GC pause spikes and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> and Memory<T> eliminate heap allocations and copy costs, but ref structs cannot be boxed or captured in async state machines.

qa.q: What is the difference between a SQL deadlock and a threading deadlock?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SQL deadlock: two transactions each holding a row/page lock the other needs — circular wait. SQL Server automatically detects and kills the "deadlock victim" with error 1205. Threading deadlock: two threads each holding a Monitor lock the other thread needs — no automatic detection, manifests as a hung application. Requires careful lock ordering or timeout-based acquisition.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

days.title: Collections internals -- List, Dictionary, HashSet under the hood
days.exp: Knowing WHAT List<T> and Dictionary<K,V> do is table stakes. Knowing HOW they work internally -- resizing behavior, hash bucket collisions, when to reach for a different collection -- is what a 4-YOE interview actually probes for.
pts: List<T> is backed by a resizable array. When capacity is exceeded, it allocates a NEW array (typically double the size) and copies every existing element over -- an O(n) operation that happens amortized rarely, but is the reason `new List<T>(expectedCount)` matters for hot paths.
`Add()` is O(1) amortized, but a single Add() call can trigger an O(n) resize. `Insert(0, item)` is always O(n) because every subsequent element must shift right.

Dictionary<K,V> is a hash table with separate chaining for collision resolution. Key lookup is O(1) average case, but degrades toward O(n) if many keys hash to the same bucket -- a bad GetHashCode() implementation can silently turn your dictionary into a linked list.

**The GetHashCode/Equals contract:** if you override Equals(), you MUST override GetHashCode() consistently -- two objects that are Equal must return the same hash code, or Dictionary/HashSet lookups will silently fail to find entries that are logically present.
HashSet<T> is literally a Dictionary<T, object> under the hood with the value discarded -- same O(1) average lookup, same hash-collision risk, same Equals/GetHashCode contract requirement.

SortedDictionary<K,V> (red-black tree, O(log n) operations, keys always enumerated in order) vs SortedList<K,V> (sorted array, O(log n) lookup via binary search but O(n) insertion due to shifting) -- know when ordered enumeration matters enough to pay the cost.
Queue<T> (FIFO) and Stack<T> (LIFO) are both backed by a resizable circular array or array respectively -- O(1) for their primary operations (Enqueue/Dequeue, Push/Pop).

ConcurrentDictionary<K,V> uses fine-grained internal locking (lock striping) rather than one global lock -- multiple threads can operate on different segments of the dictionary concurrently, unlike wrapping a regular Dictionary in a single lock statement.

qa.q: What happens internally when a List<T> exceeds its current capacity during an Add() call?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The List allocates a new backing array, typically double the previous capacity, then copies every existing element from the old array into the new one before adding the new item. This is an O(n) operation, though it happens infrequently enough that Add() is described as O(1) amortized. On a hot path adding many items, pre-sizing the List with new List<T>(expectedCount) avoids repeated resize-copy cycles entirely.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Garbage Collector uses generational collection (Gen 0, 1, 2, LOH, POH) with mark-sweep-compact phases. Span<T> provides stack-allocated contiguous representation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Excessive allocations of large objects (>85KB) trigger frequent Gen 2 / LOH collections, causing GC pause spikes and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> and Memory<T> eliminate heap allocations and copy costs, but ref structs cannot be boxed or captured in async state machines.

qa.q: Why must GetHashCode() be overridden whenever Equals() is overridden, and what breaks if you skip it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Dictionary and HashSet use GetHashCode() to determine which bucket an object belongs in, then use Equals() to confirm an exact match within that bucket. If two objects are Equal but return different hash codes, they can land in different buckets entirely -- a lookup for a logically present key can silently return 'not found' because the search never even checks the bucket the matching object is actually sitting in. This is a genuinely dangerous silent failure, not a compile error or exception.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** ServiceContainer tracks registration lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton). Scoped services are tied to an IServiceScope.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Captive dependencies (injecting a Scoped service like DbContext into a Singleton) cause state corruption, memory leaks, and multithreading race conditions.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Explicit scoping ensures request isolation, but requires IServiceScopeFactory for background hosted services.

qa.q: What is the danger of ConcurrentDictionary's GetOrAdd factory method under concurrent access?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If multiple threads call GetOrAdd for the same missing key at nearly the same time, the value factory function can be invoked more than once -- ConcurrentDictionary guarantees only one result is ultimately stored, but does not guarantee the factory itself only runs once. If the factory has side effects (an API call, a database write, incrementing an external counter), those side effects can happen multiple times even though only one value survives in the dictionary. For expensive or side-effecting factories, additional synchronization (like Lazy<T>) is needed.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** C# compiler synthesizes an IAsyncStateMachine struct. Awaiting incomplete tasks yields control to the caller; thread pool threads resume via TaskScheduler/SynchronizationContext.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Blocking async code with .Result or .Wait() on single-threaded synchronization contexts leads to deadlocks and thread pool starvation.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async preserves thread pool scalability for I/O operations, but introduces state machine allocations and complex exception bubbling.

qa.q: When would you choose SortedDictionary over SortedList, given both maintain key order?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** SortedDictionary (backed by a red-black tree) has O(log n) insertion because it doesn't need to shift elements -- it rebalances the tree instead. SortedList (backed by a sorted array) has O(log n) lookup via binary search, but O(n) insertion because inserting into the middle of the array requires shifting every subsequent element. Choose SortedDictionary when insertions/deletions are frequent; SortedList when the collection is built once and then mostly read, since arrays have better cache locality and lower memory overhead per element than a tree's node objects.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Garbage Collector uses generational collection (Gen 0, 1, 2, LOH, POH) with mark-sweep-compact phases. Span<T> provides stack-allocated contiguous representation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Excessive allocations of large objects (>85KB) trigger frequent Gen 2 / LOH collections, causing GC pause spikes and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> and Memory<T> eliminate heap allocations and copy costs, but ref structs cannot be boxed or captured in async state machines.
