days.title: Components deep dive — content projection, ViewChild, dynamic loading
days.exp: Standalone components are the standard. But senior interviews test the less-common features: multi-slot content projection, ViewChild for DOM access, TemplateRef for structural patterns, and dynamic component loading with ViewContainerRef. These appear in component library and advanced UI questions.
pts: Standalone components (`standalone: true`, default v19+) import their own dependencies — no NgModule declaration needed
`@Component` metadata: selector, template/templateUrl, styles/styleUrls, changeDetection, encapsulation
**Content projection:** `<ng-content>` projects content from the parent into the child. **Multi-slot:** `<ng-content select="[header]">` projects only elements matching the CSS selector
**`ng-container`:** grouping element that renders no DOM node — useful with `@if` / `@for` to avoid extra wrapper divs
**`ng-template`:** defines a template fragment that is not rendered by default; referenced by `TemplateRef`; used with structural directives and `ViewContainerRef`
**`@ViewChild(ref)`:** queries a child in the current component's VIEW — available in `ngAfterViewInit`. `@ViewChildren` for a list of children.
**`@ContentChild(ref)`:** queries a child projected via `<ng-content>` — available in `ngAfterContentInit`. `@ContentChildren` for a list.
**`ElementRef`:** wraps a native DOM element. Prefer Renderer2 for DOM manipulation to stay cross-platform (SSR/Web Worker safe).
**Dynamic component loading:** `ViewContainerRef.createComponent(ComponentClass)` instantiates a component at runtime — used for modals, toasts, dynamic dashboards
View encapsulation: `Emulated` (default, scoped CSS via attribute), `None` (global CSS), `ShadowDom` (native shadow DOM)

qa.q: What is the difference between @ViewChild and @ContentChild?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** @ViewChild queries elements in the component's own template (its VIEW) — the DOM it creates itself. Available after ngAfterViewInit. @ContentChild queries elements that were PROJECTED into the component via <ng-content> — content that came from the parent. Available after ngAfterContentInit. Practical: @ViewChild for finding a child component you defined in your template; @ContentChild for finding what the parent injected into your slots.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is multi-slot content projection and how do you implement it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Multi-slot content projection lets a component define multiple named slots for projected content using CSS selectors on <ng-content>. Add a select attribute: <ng-content select="[header]"> only projects elements with the header attribute, <ng-content select=".footer"> projects elements with the footer CSS class, <ng-content> (no select) is the default slot for everything else. The parent marks its projected elements with the matching attribute or class.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is ViewContainerRef and what can you do with it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ViewContainerRef is an injection token representing a position in the DOM where views (component or template instances) can be inserted. You can use it to: createComponent(Type) — dynamically instantiate and insert a component; createEmbeddedView(TemplateRef) — render an ng-template at that position; clear() — remove all dynamically created views. It's the foundation for modals, dynamic dashboards, and structural directives.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is the difference between ng-container and ng-template?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ng-container renders NO DOM element — it's a logical grouping element for applying @if, @for, or directives without adding a wrapper div. ng-template defines a template fragment that is NOT rendered at all by default — it's a blueprint that must be explicitly instantiated via ngTemplateOutlet, ViewContainerRef.createEmbeddedView(), or a structural directive. Think: ng-container is "invisible wrapper," ng-template is "stored-but-not-rendered blueprint."

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: When would you use ElementRef vs Renderer2 for DOM manipulation?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ElementRef gives you direct access to the native DOM element via nativeElement — simple but platform-specific (breaks in Server-Side Rendering or Web Workers). Renderer2 provides an abstraction layer for DOM manipulation (createElement, setAttribute, setStyle, listen) that works across all Angular platforms including SSR. Use ElementRef for read-only access or when you're certain you're in a browser context; use Renderer2 for all DOM writes to ensure SSR compatibility.

days.title: Template syntax — deferrable views, pipes, ng-template, reference variables
days.exp: Angular's @defer blocks (stable in v17) are now a core performance feature that interviewers ask about. Custom pipes, the async pipe, and template reference variables are all commonly tested. Know how to avoid the common pitfall of impure pipes breaking OnPush.
pts: **New control flow:** `@if (cond)`, `@if (cond) {} @else {}`, `@for (item of list; track item.id) {} @empty {}`, `@switch (val) { @case (x) {} @default {} }`
**`@for` must have `track`:** expression that uniquely identifies items for DOM reconciliation — without it, Angular recreates all DOM on any change
**Deferrable views `@defer`:** lazily loads a component chunk; the browser only downloads the JS when a condition is met

**`@defer` triggers:** `@defer (on viewport)` — when block enters viewport; `@defer (on idle)` — when browser is idle; `@defer (on interaction)` — on click/focus; `@defer (when condition)` — signal/expression becomes true
**`@defer` blocks:** `@placeholder` (rendered before defer), `@loading` (shown while loading), `@error` (shown if load fails)
**Pure pipes:** implement `PipeTransform`, run only when input reference changes — safe with OnPush. **Impure pipes:** run on every change detection cycle — avoid with OnPush
**`async` pipe:** subscribes to an Observable/Promise, returns current value, auto-unsubscribes on component destroy — the cleanest way to consume Observables in templates
**Template reference variables `#ref`:** reference an element, component, or directive in the template; accessible via @ViewChild or in the same template
**`ng-template` + `*ngTemplateOutlet`:** re-use a template fragment multiple times with different context variables

qa.q: What is @defer and what are its trigger options?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** @defer is a block-level template directive that lazily loads the template content (and the component classes it uses) as a separate JS chunk. It only downloads the code when a trigger condition is met. Triggers: on viewport (IntersectionObserver), on idle (requestIdleCallback), on interaction (click or focus on the placeholder), on immediate (right away, but async), on timer(n) (after n ms), when expression (signal or boolean expression). @placeholder, @loading, and @error blocks control what's shown before/during/after loading.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What is the difference between a pure and an impure pipe?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Pure pipe (pure: true, the default): Angular only re-runs the transform when the input reference changes — works well with OnPush components. Impure pipe (pure: false): Angular re-runs the transform on every change detection cycle regardless of input changes — necessary for pipes that depend on external state (like the async pipe or a pipe that reads Date.now()), but breaks OnPush optimization. Avoid impure pipes in OnPush components unless necessary.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What does the async pipe do that manually subscribing doesn't?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The async pipe: (1) subscribes to an Observable or Promise automatically, (2) returns the current emitted value for display, (3) triggers change detection when a new value arrives (compatible with OnPush), and (4) automatically unsubscribes when the component is destroyed — preventing memory leaks. Manual subscribe() in the component requires explicit unsubscribe in ngOnDestroy; forgetting causes memory leaks. The async pipe is the preferred pattern for template-bound streams.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: What is a template reference variable and how is it used?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A template reference variable (#ref) is a name given to an element, component, or directive in the template. Inside the template, you can use #myInput on an <input> and then reference it as myInput.value in event handlers. Combined with @ViewChild('myInput') in the component class, you can access the element programmatically after the view is initialized. They're also used to reference child components: #myModal gives access to the MyModalComponent's public API.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is @for's track and what happens without it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** track is an expression that uniquely identifies each item in the list — Angular uses it to associate DOM elements with data items across re-renders. With track item.id: when the list changes, Angular only updates DOM nodes whose items actually changed. Without track: Angular must destroy and recreate ALL DOM nodes on any list change (since it can't tell what moved vs what changed). Missing track is a compile error in Angular 17+ (unlike *ngFor where trackBy was optional).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

days.title: Dependency injection deep dive — tokens, hierarchical DI, factories
days.exp: Most Angular developers know basic @Injectable DI but struggle with InjectionToken, multi-providers, and hierarchical injectors. These are tested in library authoring and architecture questions — and they explain some Angular behaviours that otherwise seem like magic.
pts: `@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })` — registers at the root injector; singleton; tree-shakeable
`providers` in `@Component` metadata — creates a new instance of the service for that component and its children; not a singleton
**Hierarchical injectors:** root injector → environment injectors (lazy-loaded modules) → component injectors (each component can override). Resolution walks up the tree.
**`InjectionToken<T>`:** for providing non-class values (strings, config objects, functions, primitives) via DI
**`useClass`:** provide a different implementation. **`useValue`:** provide a literal value. **`useFactory`:** provide a value from a factory function. **`useExisting`:** alias one token to another.
**Multi-providers:** `multi: true` — multiple providers for the same token return an array. Used for HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, VALIDATORS, and extensible plugin systems.
**`inject()` function:** call inside constructor, factory functions, or injection context (not in lifecycle hooks); preferred over constructor injection in modern Angular
**`@Optional()`:** inject returns null if not provided. **`@Self()`:** only look in the component's own injector. **`@SkipSelf()`:** skip current injector, go straight to parent.
**`@Host()`:** look only up to the host element's injector — useful in directives

qa.q: What is an InjectionToken and when do you use it instead of a class?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** InjectionToken<T> is a typed token for providing non-class values via Angular's DI system — strings, numbers, config objects, factory functions, or anything that isn't a class. Example: const API_URL = new InjectionToken<string>('api.url'). You use it because Angular's DI uses types as keys, and there's no type key for a primitive. InjectionTokens also work for providing different implementations of the same interface without a concrete class as the token.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What are multi-providers and what are they used for?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Multi-providers let multiple providers register under the same token, and the injected value is an array of all registered values. Add multi: true to each provider. Angular uses this pattern for HTTP_INTERCEPTORS (register multiple interceptors that all run), VALIDATORS (multiple validator factories), and extensible plugin systems. Without multi: true, later providers overwrite earlier ones. With multi: true, all are collected into an array.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: How does hierarchical DI work in Angular?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Angular has a tree of injectors mirroring the component tree. When you inject a service, Angular walks up the injector tree: component injector → parent component injector → ... → environment injector → root injector. If a component provides a service in its providers array, it (and its children) get a new instance, not the root singleton. This enables component-scoped state. @Self() limits lookup to the current component's injector; @SkipSelf() skips it and goes to the parent; @Optional() returns null instead of throwing if not found.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is the difference between useClass, useValue, useFactory, and useExisting?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** useClass: provide an instance of a different class than the token — { provide: Logger, useClass: ConsoleLogger }. useValue: provide a static value directly — { provide: API_URL, useValue: '/api/v2' }. useFactory: compute the provided value via a function that can inject its own dependencies — { provide: Logger, useFactory: (env: Env) => env.prod ? new SilentLogger() : new ConsoleLogger(), deps: [Env] }. useExisting: alias one token to an already-registered token — { provide: OldService, useExisting: NewService }.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is the inject() function and when do you use it instead of constructor injection?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** inject(Token) is a function-based alternative to constructor injection, usable inside the injection context: constructor body, field initializers, factory functions, and functional guards/interceptors. It's preferred in modern Angular because: (1) it's less ceremony for simple injections, (2) works in functional constructs (guards, interceptors) that have no class constructor, and (3) it's required inside inject()-based factory providers. It cannot be used in lifecycle hooks (outside the injection context).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

days.title: RxJS operators — comprehensive deep dive
days.exp: Most Angular developers know map, filter, switchMap. Senior interviews probe the less-common operators: combineLatest, forkJoin, exhaustMap, shareReplay, catchError with retry. Each has specific semantics that matter — using the wrong operator causes subtle bugs.
pts: `switchMap`: on each source emission, unsubscribes from previous inner observable, subscribes to new one. Use: search-as-you-type, navigation (cancel previous request on new route).
`mergeMap` (=`flatMap`): all inner observables run concurrently. Use: parallel uploads, fire-and-forget side effects.
`concatMap`: queues inner observables, waits for each to complete before starting next. Use: sequential operations where ORDER matters (save then notify).
`exhaustMap`: ignores new emissions while current inner observable is active. Use: login button (ignore double-clicks while login is in progress).
`combineLatest([a$, b$])`: emits when ANY source emits, combining latest values from ALL sources. Use: combining filter selection with data stream.
`forkJoin([a$, b$])`: waits for ALL observables to complete, then emits an array of their LAST values. Use: parallel HTTP calls that must all finish before proceeding (like Promise.all).
`zip([a$, b$])`: emits only when ALL sources have each emitted a new value — pairs nth emissions. Rarely needed.
`shareReplay(1)`: multicasts the observable to multiple subscribers AND replays the last emission to late subscribers — use to share HTTP responses without re-fetching.
`catchError(err => of(fallback))`: handle errors inline, return a replacement observable to continue the stream.
`retry(n)` / `retryWhen(errors => errors.pipe(delay(1000)))`: retry on error with optional backoff.
`debounceTime(300)`: emit only after n ms of silence — search input. `throttleTime(1000)`: emit immediately, then ignore for n ms — scroll events.

qa.q: What is the difference between switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, and exhaustMap?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** All four project source emissions to inner observables but handle concurrency differently. switchMap: cancels the previous inner observable when a new source emission arrives — use for search/autocomplete. mergeMap: runs all inner observables simultaneously — use for parallel independent operations. concatMap: queues inner observables, starts the next only after the previous completes — use when order matters. exhaustMap: ignores new source emissions while an inner observable is active — use for preventing duplicate requests (login button, submit forms).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: What is the difference between forkJoin and combineLatest?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** forkJoin waits for all source observables to COMPLETE, then emits once with an array/object of their final values — like Promise.all(). Use for parallel HTTP calls that must all finish. combineLatest emits whenever ANY source emits, combining the LATEST value from all sources — it never "finishes." Use for reactive forms, filter combinations, or any scenario where you need the latest from multiple ongoing streams combined into one.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: What does shareReplay(1) do and why is it important for services?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** shareReplay(1) multicasts an observable (so multiple subscribers share one upstream subscription) and caches the last n emissions, replaying them to new late subscribers. Without it, if two components both subscribe to this.http.get('/api/me'), Angular makes two HTTP calls. With shareReplay(1), the first subscriber triggers the HTTP call; subsequent subscribers get the cached response immediately without another network request. Essential for any service-level data stream that is shared across the app.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: How do you handle errors in an RxJS pipeline without breaking the stream?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use catchError inside a switchMap or mergeMap (not at the top level): source$.pipe(switchMap(x => apiCall(x).pipe(catchError(() => of(fallback)))). This way, an error in one inner call returns a fallback value, and the outer stream continues listening. If you put catchError at the top level, an error terminates the entire stream (including the outer subscription). The of(fallback) is typically of([]) for lists or of(null) for optional data.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: When would you use debounceTime vs throttleTime?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** debounceTime(n): wait until n milliseconds of silence, then emit — use for search inputs where you want to wait until the user stops typing before making an API call. throttleTime(n): emit immediately, then ignore emissions for n milliseconds — use for scroll or resize events where you want immediate response but need to limit the rate. debounceTime delays all emissions; throttleTime passes the first and drops the rest during the throttle window.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

days.title: Signals — complete API: toSignal, toObservable, resource, model
days.exp: Signals were introduced in v16 and are now the primary state primitive in Angular. At 4 YOE, know the full API including the interop layer (toSignal/toObservable), the resource API (stable v22), and the model() two-way binding signal. These appear in any Angular round that goes beyond basics.
pts: `signal(init)` — read: `count()`. Write: `.set(val)` or `.update(fn)`. Mutation: `.mutate(fn)` for objects (signals track by reference).
`computed(() => ...)` — pure derived signal; memoized; lazy; re-calculates only when dependencies change and something reads it
`effect(() => ...)` — side effect that runs when its signal dependencies change; impure; runs at least once; cleanup via returned function
`linkedSignal({ source, computation })` — writable signal that resets when source changes (stable v20)
**`toSignal(obs$)`:** converts an Observable to a signal; subscribes automatically; optionally accepts `initialValue` or `requireSync` option
**`toObservable(signal)`:** converts a signal to an Observable; emits each time the signal's value changes
**`resource()` / `rxResource()` / `httpResource()`:** reactive data-fetching primitives (stable v22); return `value()`, `isLoading()`, `error()` signals; re-fetch when input signals change
**`model<T>()`:** a two-way bindable signal input; replaces @Input() + @Output() EventEmitter for parent-child two-way binding; parent binds with `[(myProp)]="signal"`
**`untracked(fn)`:** call a signal inside an effect or computed without creating a dependency — use when you need to read a signal for its value but don't want the effect to re-run when it changes
**Signal effects cleanup:** return a cleanup function from effect() for subscriptions, timers, or event listeners that need teardown

qa.q: What does toSignal() do and when would you use it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** toSignal(observable$) subscribes to an Observable and returns a signal that reflects its latest emitted value. Angular manages the subscription and unsubscribes on destroy. Use it when you have a service that returns an Observable but your component is signal-based and you want to use the value in a template or computed() without the async pipe. Options: initialValue (value before first emission), requireSync (throws if the Observable doesn't emit synchronously).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What is httpResource() and how does it differ from using HttpClient directly?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** httpResource<T>(urlFn) creates a reactive data loader where the URL is a computed function of signals. It automatically re-fetches when any signal the URL function reads changes. It returns an object with value() (the data), isLoading() (boolean signal), and error() (error signal) — all signals. Compared to HttpClient + switchMap: httpResource needs ~3 lines vs ~10; no pipe, no subscribe, no takeUntilDestroyed. HttpClient + switchMap is still better for complex scenarios needing RxJS operators (debounce, retry, catchError).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What is model() and what does it replace?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** model<T>() is a signal-based alternative to the @Input() + @Output() EventEmitter pattern for two-way binding. In the child: checked = model(false) creates a writable signal that also emits on .set(). In the parent: <toggle [(checked)]="mySignal" /> binds the signal two-ways. It replaces the verbose pattern of @Input() checked and @Output() checkedChange = new EventEmitter<boolean>() with valueChange$. model() is cleaner, type-safe, and signal-native.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: What is untracked() and when do you use it inside an effect?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** untracked(fn) reads a signal inside an effect or computed without registering it as a dependency. Normally, every signal read inside effect() adds that signal as a dependency — the effect re-runs when any dependency changes. untracked lets you read a signal for its current value without making the effect reactive to that signal. Use it when you need to sample a signal's value at the moment the effect runs, but you don't want that signal to trigger a re-run.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What is the difference between computed() and effect() in terms of execution?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** computed() is lazy — it only re-evaluates when something reads it AND at least one of its dependencies changed. It's memoized: if the same dependencies changed but the computed result hasn't changed, Angular may skip re-rendering. effect() is eager — it runs automatically whenever any of its signal dependencies change, whether or not anything is reading its result. effect() is for side effects (logging, local storage writes, imperative DOM), not for deriving values (use computed() for that).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

days.title: Routing — resolvers, preloading, animations, named outlets
days.exp: Most developers know basic routing. Senior interviews probe resolvers (data before navigation), preloading strategies (performance), and how to handle complex multi-view layouts with named router outlets. Route animations are occasionally tested for UI roles.
pts: **Functional guards** (`canActivate`, `canDeactivate`, `canMatch`): replace class-based guards — just a function returning `true`, `false`, or a `UrlTree`
**`canDeactivate`:** warns user before leaving a form with unsaved changes — confirm with signal or user prompt
**Route resolver:** fetches data BEFORE navigating; the component receives it via `ActivatedRoute.data`; if it throws, navigation is cancelled
**Functional resolver:** `ResolveFn<T>` — just a function, no class needed (Angular 15+)

**Preloading strategies:** `NoPreloading` (default, load on demand), `PreloadAllModules` (preload all lazily loaded routes after initial render), custom (preload specific routes based on data/network)
**`withPreloading(PreloadAllModules)`:** in `provideRouter()` — preloads all lazy routes immediately after the app boots
**Named router outlets:** `<router-outlet name="sidebar">` — multiple outlets in one template for auxiliary routes (sidepanels, modals)
**Route animations:** trigger animations on route change by binding `@routeAnimation` to the `outlet` element and reading `activatedRoute.data.animation`
**`ActivatedRoute`:** inject to access `params`, `queryParams`, `data`, `url`, `snapshot`, `parent` — use `Signal` versions in v17.3+: `route.input('id')`

qa.q: What is a route resolver and why use it instead of loading data in ngOnInit?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A resolver is a function that fetches data before Angular completes navigation to a route. The component only instantiates after the resolver completes. Benefits: the component always has its data available immediately (no loading spinner, no conditional template), and if the resolver throws or returns an empty observable, navigation is cancelled (the user never sees a broken component). Downside: the route change is delayed until the resolver completes — consider showing a global loading indicator.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: What is the difference between NoPreloading and PreloadAllModules?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** NoPreloading (default): lazy routes are only loaded when the user navigates to them — best for large apps where most users don't visit all routes. PreloadAllModules: after the initial app loads, Angular immediately begins preloading ALL lazy route bundles in the background — subsequent navigations feel instant because the chunks are already downloaded. Use PreloadAllModules for smaller apps or admin panels where users are likely to visit multiple sections.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What are named router outlets and what are they used for?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Named router outlets allow multiple router-outlet elements in one template, each rendering a different route simultaneously. Syntax: <router-outlet name="sidebar"></router-outlet>. Navigate to a named outlet: router.navigate([{ outlets: { primary: ['home'], sidebar: ['user-info'] } }]). Use for auxiliary views that change independently of the main content — a sidebar with contextual info, a modal that has its own URL, or a split-pane layout.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: How do functional route guards work compared to class-based guards?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Functional guards are plain functions typed as CanActivateFn, CanDeactivateFn, etc. They use inject() internally to access services. Advantages: no class boilerplate (no implements, no class declaration), composable (you can call one functional guard from another), and naturally tree-shakeable. Class-based guards still work but require the class to be provided — functional guards are the Angular 15+ standard and the approach in all new Angular docs.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: How do you access route parameters as signals in Angular 17.3+?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** In Angular 17.3+, ActivatedRoute exposes signal-based accessors: inject(ActivatedRoute).snapshot.paramMap is the static snapshot. For reactive access with signals: use the input() function with routerLink inputs when the component is registered with the router using withComponentInputBinding() in provideRouter(). This maps route params/queryParams directly to component inputs, which can be signal-based inputs: userId = input<string>('userId').

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

days.title: Forms deep dive — ControlValueAccessor, async validators, complex patterns
days.exp: Beyond the basics, interviewers test ControlValueAccessor (create a custom form control), async validators (server-side email check), and cross-field validation. These are the patterns that appear in UI library and enterprise form-heavy Angular work.
pts: `FormGroup`, `FormControl`, `FormArray` — the three building blocks of Reactive Forms
**Typed Forms** (Angular 14+): `FormGroup<{email: FormControl<string>}>` — TypeScript knows the shape of each control; use `nonNullable: true` to avoid `T | null` types
**`FormBuilder`** shorthand: `this.fb.nonNullable.group({ email: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.email]] })`
**Custom validator:** `ValidatorFn` that returns `ValidationErrors | null` — return `null` for valid, an object for invalid
**Cross-field validator:** set on a `FormGroup`, receives the entire group — use to compare two fields (passwords match, date range valid)
**Async validator:** `AsyncValidatorFn` returning `Observable<ValidationErrors | null>` — debounce to avoid hammering the server on every keystroke
**`updateOn`:** control when validation runs: `updateOn: 'change'` (default), `'blur'` (after leaving field), `'submit'` (on form submit only)
**`ControlValueAccessor`:** interface that makes a custom component work as a native form control — implement `writeValue`, `registerOnChange`, `registerOnTouched`, provide `NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR`
**Status:** `VALID`, `INVALID`, `PENDING` (async validator running), `DISABLED`
**`getRawValue()` vs `value`:** `value` excludes disabled controls; `getRawValue()` includes them — use getRawValue() when submitting to avoid losing disabled field data

qa.q: What is ControlValueAccessor and when do you need to implement it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** ControlValueAccessor is an interface that bridges a custom component to Angular's form API, making it usable as a form control with both Reactive Forms and template-driven Forms. You implement it when you're building a custom input component (star rating, color picker, address form, rich text editor) that should participate in form validation and value binding. Implement writeValue (receive value from form), registerOnChange (notify form of changes), registerOnTouched (notify form of blur), and provide NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR via multi-provider.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is the difference between form.value and form.getRawValue()?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** form.value excludes disabled controls — their values are omitted from the object. form.getRawValue() includes all controls including disabled ones. This matters when you disable a field for UI reasons (e.g., "confirmation email is read-only") but still need its value when submitting. If you use form.value to build the submit payload, you'll silently lose the disabled field's value. Always use getRawValue() when building the submit payload.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: How do you implement an async validator that checks if an email is already taken?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Create an AsyncValidatorFn that returns an Observable<ValidationErrors | null>: take the control value, debounce to avoid hitting the API on every keystroke, call the API, map the response to null (valid) or { emailTaken: true } (invalid). Always add catchError(() => of(null)) so an API failure doesn't break the form. The form control shows status PENDING while the async validator is running. Attach it with asyncValidators in the FormControl constructor.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: What is a cross-field validator and how do you apply it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** A cross-field validator is a ValidatorFn applied to a FormGroup (not a single FormControl) that can compare multiple fields. Example: passwords match validator receives the entire FormGroup, reads group.get('password')?.value and group.get('confirmPassword')?.value, returns null if they match or { passwordMismatch: true } if not. Apply it in the FormGroup constructor's second argument: new FormGroup({...}, { validators: [passwordMatchValidator] }). Check the error on the group: form.errors?.'passwordMismatch'.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is updateOn and what are the three options?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** updateOn controls when Angular runs validation and updates the form control value. 'change' (default): validates on every keystroke — good for instant feedback. 'blur': validates when the user leaves the field — reduces unnecessary validation noise during typing. 'submit': validates only when the form is submitted — best for sensitive fields where showing errors while typing feels intrusive. Set it per-control: new FormControl('', { updateOn: 'blur' }) or per-group: new FormGroup({...}, { updateOn: 'blur' }).

days.title: HTTP, interceptors, retry logic, and caching
days.exp: HTTP interceptors — now functional in Angular 15+ — are asked in every enterprise Angular interview. Auth token injection, global error handling, and retry-with-backoff are the three patterns you must implement fluently.
pts: **`HttpClient`:** Angular's HTTP service; all methods return Observables; supports typed responses: `http.get<User[]>('/api/users')`
**Functional interceptors** (`HttpInterceptorFn`, Angular 15+): replace class-based interceptors; registered with `withInterceptors([fn1, fn2])` in `provideHttpClient()`
**Interceptor order:** request flows through interceptors in registration order; response flows in reverse (like middleware)
**Auth interceptor:** clone the request to add Authorization header — `req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: 'Bearer ' + token } })`
**Error interceptor:** catch HTTP errors globally, show toast, refresh token on 401, redirect to login on 403
**Retry with exponential backoff:** `retryWhen(errors => errors.pipe(delayWhen((e, i) => timer(Math.pow(2,i)*1000))))` or the newer `retry({ count: 3, delay: ... })`
**Caching interceptor:** check a Map before passing through; store response in Map; return cached response for subsequent identical GET requests
**Loading interceptor:** increment/decrement a counter signal to show/hide a global spinner without modifying individual components
**`HttpContext`:** pass metadata into interceptors without modifying the service call; use `HttpContextToken<T>` to tag specific requests

qa.q: What is the difference between class-based and functional HTTP interceptors?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Class-based interceptors implement HttpInterceptor with an intercept(req, next) method and are provided with { provide: HTTP_INTERCEPTORS, useClass: ..., multi: true }. Functional interceptors are plain functions of type HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => Observable<HttpEvent<unknown>> and are registered with withInterceptors([fn]) in provideHttpClient(). Functional interceptors are cleaner (no class boilerplate), work with inject() for dependencies, are the Angular 15+ standard, and are what new Angular docs use.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: Why must you clone the request in an interceptor instead of modifying it directly?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** HttpRequest objects are immutable by design — Angular makes requests immutable so that interceptors in a chain cannot interfere with each other through shared mutation. req.clone({ setHeaders: {...} }) creates a new request with the modified properties while copying everything else. This ensures each interceptor gets a clean, unmodified request, and later interceptors see the modifications from earlier ones as intended, not accidental side effects.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: How do you implement token refresh on a 401 response in an interceptor?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Catch the 401 in catchError, call auth.refreshToken() to get a new token, then retry the original request with the new token using switchMap. The key: save the original request before the error, and re-clone it with the new Authorization header in the switchMap. Edge case: if the refresh itself returns 401 (refresh token also expired), catch that error and redirect to login. Also consider preventing parallel refresh calls if multiple requests 401 simultaneously (use a BehaviorSubject or share() to broadcast the single refresh).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Observables push events asynchronously over time. Operators (switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap) transform streams via push-based notifications.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Unsubscribed long-lived observables (e.g. interval, HTTP, Store) create severe memory leaks when components destroy.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** switchMap cancels previous pending requests ideal for search auto-complete, whereas mergeMap executes all concurrently.

qa.q: What is HttpContext and why is it useful for interceptors?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** HttpContext lets you attach metadata to an HTTP request that interceptors can read, without modifying the request URL or headers. Define a token: const SKIP_AUTH = new HttpContextToken<boolean>(() => false). Pass it: http.get(url, { context: new HttpContext().set(SKIP_AUTH, true) }). Read in interceptor: req.context.get(SKIP_AUTH). Use cases: skip auth for public endpoints, skip caching for specific calls, mark a request as high-priority, or pass any interceptor-specific configuration without polluting the service call signature.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: How do you implement a caching interceptor for GET requests?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Maintain a Map<string, HttpResponse> in a singleton service. In the interceptor: if the request is a GET and the URL is in the cache, return of(cachedResponse) and skip next(req). Otherwise, call next(req), tap the response to store it in the cache, and return the response. Add cache invalidation: either time-based (TTL via Date.now()), or explicit (clear the cache entry when a related mutation request succeeds). Only cache GET requests — POST/PUT/DELETE should never be cached.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

days.title: Change detection — complete deep dive, zoneless migration strategy
days.exp: Change detection is the most misunderstood Angular internals topic. At 4 YOE, you need to explain not just 'OnPush is faster' but exactly when OnPush triggers, what Zone.js actually does, and how to migrate to zoneless — a question now appearing in senior Angular interviews.
pts: **Zone.js:** monkey-patches all browser async APIs (setTimeout, Promise, fetch, addEventListener) and fires `ApplicationRef.tick()` after each — triggering a full tree check
**Default strategy:** Angular checks EVERY component on every tick — even components that couldn't possibly have changed. Simple but inefficient at scale.

**OnPush triggers (exactly 4):** (1) an `@Input` reference changes, (2) an `async` pipe in the template emits a new value, (3) a signal the template reads updates, (4) `ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()` is called manually
**`ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges()`:** immediately check this component and its children — synchronous; use when you've mutated data outside Angular's awareness
**`ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck()`:** mark this component and ancestors as dirty — they will be checked on the NEXT tick; use with OnPush + Observables
**`NgZone.runOutsideAngular(fn)`:** run code without triggering change detection — use for performance-intensive loops, WebSockets, chart libraries
**`NgZone.run(fn)`:** re-enter Angular zone from outside — use after an outside-zone callback that needs to update the UI
**Zoneless (Angular 21+, default for new projects):** no Zone.js dependency; change detection driven entirely by signals; enables true SSR/Web Worker compatibility
**Zoneless migration:** enable OnPush everywhere → replace property mutations with signal.set() → add provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection() → test → remove zone.js from polyfills

qa.q: What does Zone.js actually do and why is Angular removing it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Zone.js monkey-patches browser async APIs at startup: setTimeout, Promise, fetch, XMLHttpRequest, addEventListener, etc. When any patched API completes, Zone.js fires a notification and Angular calls ApplicationRef.tick() — which checks every component in the tree for changes. It's magic: no code changes needed, but it causes performance issues (full-tree check after every async operation, even trivial ones like setTimeout(fn, 0)) and breaks with non-Angular libraries that also patch these APIs. Signals provide a targeted alternative — Angular knows exactly which components to update.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What are the four exact conditions that trigger OnPush change detection?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1) An @Input reference changes (object identity changes, not object mutation). 2) An async pipe in the template emits a new value. 3) A signal that the template reads (signal()) updates — Angular tracks signal reads at the component level. 4) ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck() is called explicitly. Mutations to objects/arrays without changing reference (arr.push()) do NOT trigger OnPush — you must reassign: this.arr.set([...this.arr(), newItem]) for signals, or this.cdr.markForCheck() for non-signal patterns.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What is the difference between ChangeDetectorRef.detectChanges() and markForCheck()?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** detectChanges() is synchronous — it immediately checks the current component and its children right now, in the current call stack. Use when you've updated state from outside Angular's knowledge and need immediate UI update. markForCheck() is asynchronous — it marks the component (and its ancestors in the tree) as dirty, to be checked on the next change detection cycle triggered by Zone.js or ApplicationRef.tick(). Use in OnPush components that receive data via Observables or external callbacks.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What is NgZone.runOutsideAngular and when do you use it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** NgZone.runOutsideAngular(fn) executes code in a context where Zone.js does not trigger change detection. Use it for: requestAnimationFrame loops for canvas/chart animations (prevent CD on every frame), WebSocket message handling that updates a buffer before signaling Angular, third-party library initialization that fires many callbacks, or any computation where you only need to update Angular's view at the end (call zone.run(() => signal.set(result)) when done).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.

qa.q: What are the steps to migrate an existing Angular app to zoneless?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1) Add provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection() to the providers array. 2) Enable OnPush on all components. 3) Replace all mutable property assignments that trigger CD with signal.set(). 4) Replace remaining manual markForCheck() calls with signal updates. 5) Test — components that relied on Zone.js detecting property mutations will stop updating (surfaces hidden bugs). 6) Remove zone.js from polyfills.ts and package.json. This can be incremental: Zone.js and zoneless signals coexist during migration.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

days.title: Performance — @defer, virtual scroll, trackBy, pure pipes, bundle analysis
days.exp: Performance optimisation is a guaranteed senior topic. Beyond OnPush (covered in Day 9), know @defer for code-splitting, CDK virtual scroll for long lists, and bundle analysis with angular-bundle-analyzer — these distinguish candidates who have shipped at scale.
pts: **@defer (stable v17):** lazy-loads components and their dependencies as a separate JS chunk; reduces initial bundle size
**Triggers: `on viewport`** (IntersectionObserver), **`on idle`** (requestIdleCallback), **`on interaction`** (click/focus), **`when signal()`** (programmatic), **`on immediate`** (async, next tick)
**`@defer (prefetch on idle)`:** preloads the chunk in the background when idle — downloaded before needed, renders faster when triggered
**Virtual scrolling (CDK):** `<cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport itemSize="50">` — only renders DOM for visible rows; essential for lists of 1000+ items
**`trackBy` in `@for`:** `track item.id` — Angular reuses existing DOM elements for unchanged items instead of recreating all
**Pure pipes for computed display values:** computed logic in the template without side effects; safer than computing in the template expression and faster than impure pipes
**`NgOptimizedImage` (`[ngSrc]`):** Angular image directive; adds `loading="lazy"`, `fetchpriority`, `srcset`, and size hints automatically; enforces best practices
**Bundle analysis:** `ng build --stats-json && npx webpack-bundle-analyzer dist/*/stats.json` — visualise chunk sizes and find large dependencies to lazy-load
**Standalone component tree-shaking:** unused components are excluded from the bundle automatically when not imported — NgModules prevented this

qa.q: What is the difference between @defer triggers on viewport and on idle?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** on viewport: Angular uses IntersectionObserver to detect when the @placeholder element enters the browser viewport — then downloads and renders the deferred content. Best for below-the-fold content. on idle: uses requestIdleCallback to defer loading until the browser has nothing else to do — content loads soon after initial render but without blocking the main thread. Best for non-critical widgets that can load any time. You can combine them: @defer (on viewport; prefetch on idle) — preloads the chunk when idle, renders immediately when scrolled into view.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: When is CDK virtual scroll necessary vs a simple @for loop?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use CDK virtual scroll when rendering more than ~500-1000 items in a list that the user can scroll through. With @for and 10,000 items, Angular creates 10,000 DOM nodes — heavy initial render, slow scroll, memory-intensive. CDK virtual scroll only creates DOM nodes for the visible items (typically 10-20) plus a small buffer, regardless of list size. The viewport knows the item size (itemSize="48" in pixels) to calculate total scroll height without rendering all items.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: Why should heavy computed values be in pure pipes rather than template expressions?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Template expressions like {{ computeHeavyValue(item) }} re-evaluate on EVERY change detection cycle — even if item hasn't changed — because Angular can't know whether the function's output has changed without calling it. A pure pipe runs only when its input REFERENCE changes, memoizing the result. This means for OnPush components, the pipe computation skips when @Input doesn't change. Additionally, pipes are composable and testable in isolation, while template function calls are not.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.

qa.q: What is NgOptimizedImage and what problems does it solve automatically?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** NgOptimizedImage ([ngSrc]) is a built-in Angular directive for image optimization. It automatically: adds loading="lazy" for below-fold images (reduces initial page load), adds fetchpriority="high" for images marked as [priority] (LCP elements), generates a srcset for responsive images, enforces explicit width/height attributes to prevent layout shift (CLS), and warns in dev mode about images that are sized incorrectly. It removes the need for manual optimization that developers frequently forget.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: How do you analyse bundle size in an Angular app?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Run ng build --stats-json to generate a webpack stats file. Then run npx webpack-bundle-analyzer dist/your-app/stats.json to open an interactive treemap showing which modules contribute most to each chunk. Look for: unexpectedly large dependencies (moment.js, lodash), large vendor chunks that should be split, lazy route chunks that are too large (split further), and shared chunks that might benefit from optimization. Angular 17+ also shows chunk sizes in the build output.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

days.title: Testing — TestBed, Vitest (v21+), component harnesses, mocking
days.exp: Angular testing is tested less often in product company interviews but is a common question at companies that prioritize quality. Know TestBed setup, how to test OnPush components, how to mock services, and the Vitest setup (Angular 21+). Signal-based testing patterns are now relevant.
pts: **`TestBed.configureTestingModule`:** sets up an Angular testing environment; declare the component under test and its dependencies (real or mocked)
**`ComponentFixture<T>`:** wrapper around the component; `.componentInstance` (component class), `.nativeElement` (DOM), `.detectChanges()` (trigger CD)
**Testing OnPush:** must call `fixture.detectChanges()` after every state change — OnPush doesn't auto-detect outside the test context
**Mock services:** `jasmine.createSpyObj('UserService', ['getUser'])` or a plain object with jest/vitest `vi.fn()` methods
**`HttpClientTestingModule` / `provideHttpClientTesting()`:** provides a test implementation of HttpClient; use `HttpTestingController.expectOne(url)` to intercept and respond
**Component harnesses (CDK):** `HarnessLoader.getHarness(MatButtonHarness)` — interact with Material components in tests through a stable API instead of fragile DOM selectors
**Testing signals:** signals work synchronously in tests — `component.count.set(5); fixture.detectChanges(); expect(el.textContent).toBe('5')`
**Vitest (Angular 21+, default):** replaces Karma; faster, runs in Node.js; configure via `vitest.config.ts`; uses `describe`, `it`, `expect` like Jest
**`fakeAsync` + `tick(n)`:** fake time to test debounced or delayed operations without real waiting

qa.q: What is the difference between shallow and deep component testing in Angular?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Shallow testing (using NO_ERRORS_SCHEMA or stub children): only the component under test is fully rendered; child components are replaced with empty stubs. Faster and more isolated but doesn't verify integration with children. Deep testing (declaring all child components): renders the full component tree. More realistic but slower and more fragile. For unit tests, shallow is preferred; for integration tests that verify component composition, deep is appropriate. The Angular CDK HarnessLoader provides a middle ground for testing specific child component interactions.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: Why do you need to call fixture.detectChanges() in Angular tests?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Angular does not run change detection automatically in the test environment. fixture.detectChanges() triggers one round of change detection: it initialises the component (ngOnInit runs on the first call), then updates the DOM to reflect the current component state. For OnPush components, you MUST call detectChanges() after every state change or the template won't update. Always call it: once in beforeEach after creating the component (initial render), and once after every state change in test cases.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: What is the Angular CDK component harness and why use it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** CDK component harnesses provide a stable API for testing components — especially Angular Material components. Instead of querying the DOM directly (fixture.nativeElement.querySelector('.mat-button')), which breaks when Material changes its DOM structure, you use HarnessLoader.getHarness(MatButtonHarness) and call harness.click(). Benefits: tests are decoupled from implementation details, work consistently across browsers, and don't break on Material version upgrades. You can also write custom harnesses for your own components.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** T-SQL engine parses, compiles into execution plans, caches them in the plan cache, and executes via the storage engine (buffer pool & latching).

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Parameter sniffing and missing stats cause sub-optimal plan compilation, resulting in full table scans and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Parameterization improves plan reuse, but recompile hints (OPTION RECOMPILE) may be needed for skewed data distributions.

qa.q: How does Vitest differ from Karma for Angular tests?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Karma launches a real browser (Chrome/Firefox), runs tests inside it, and reports results back — slow startup, requires a display. Vitest runs in Node.js using jsdom for DOM simulation — starts in milliseconds, runs tests in parallel, and integrates with the Vite build pipeline. Vitest is up to 10x faster for unit tests. Angular 21 made Vitest the default test runner for new projects. The test syntax is nearly identical (describe/it/expect) — the main migration work is configuration and replacing Karma-specific setup.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Angular compiler generates Ivy instructions, linking component templates to DOM nodes with change detection dirty checking.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing heavy computations inside template expressions runs on every change detection cycle, causing UI lag.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** OnPush change detection skips subtrees unless inputs change, drastically improving performance at the cost of strict immutability.

qa.q: How do you test a component that uses signals?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Signals are synchronous — reading and setting them is immediate, unlike Observables. To test: set the signal value with component.mySignal.set(value); call fixture.detectChanges(); then assert on the DOM. For computed signals: set the source signals, call detectChanges, assert the computed result. For effects: effects run during change detection, so fixture.detectChanges() is enough to trigger them. Signal-based tests are generally simpler than Observable-based tests because there's no async, no tick, no subscribe needed for state changes.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Signals build a fine-grained reactive dependency graph. When a signal value changes, only dependent view nodes are scheduled for DOM updating.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Mutating signal values inside effects without untracked() causes infinite change detection loops and browser freeze.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Signals provide predictable synchronous reactivity without Zone.js overhead, but require adapting existing RxJS-heavy codebases.
